news.title: US grounds all flights for hours, sparking travel chaos
news.text:
The US grounded all flights for several hours Saturday, sparking travel chaos across the vast country, after what government officials said was a major communications outage caused by decades old technology.

The nationwide stop left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace since the 9/11 attacks.

Federal Aviation Authority officials lifted the groundstop after around four hours, with President Donald Trump’s administration saying there was no evidence the outage was the result of foul play.

“This is a legacy system problem,” said Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. “We have old, old switches, old routers.

“We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down, and went down everywhere. It got overloaded.”

Duffy on Thursday had formally asked Congress for $30.1 billion in funds to upgrade and modernise the US Air Traffic Control System.

As the groundstop was lifted he repeated his plea.

“I’m going to say it a million times: the Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this bill,” he said.

6,000 flights canceled

With almost 6,000 flights canceled including some international routes according to FlightAware, the recovery from the stoppage was expected to take some time.

Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways.

Passengers thronged concorses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their travel plans into chaos.

“We’re trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too,” said Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California.

US airspace is among the busiest in the world, and is ramping up to its most frenetic as the Thanksgiving holiday moves into view.

A nationwide groundstop is highly unusual; there was one such stop in January 2023 when a pilot notification system failed, but the only other national stop happened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, when no aircraft took to the skies for days.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday.

“We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyber attack or (AI) attack,” he told a press conference.

He also ruled out any connection with the outage that affected Microsoft this week, knocking email systems offline for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide.

Confusion and delays

The stop sparked chaos and misery at airports around the country.

At New York’s LaGuardia Airport, Tiara Johnson said she had been trying to get to Orlando for a concert with a friend.

“They just keep delaying it…So it started out at 7:55. Then it went to 8:30, 9:30. Now it’s at 10:30. So we don’t know when it’s gonna leave,” she told AFP.

“I feel very frustrated because you know, you come to the airport and then all of a sudden your whole plans have changed and you don’t know when you’re leaving. We’re kind of stuck.”

Travelers were left in the dark on the groundstop, with some saying they had been told their flight was delayed because of wind, while others were left to gather what information they could.

Boards at the airport continued to show departures leaving as normal, while mobile boarding passes held by those stuck on the ground appeared to show their flight was underway.

Stranded passengers were scrambling to find alternatives, with long lines forming at rental car counters at the airport in Las Vegas.

Susan Sardina said she had boarded her flight back to Orange County, California when staff told passengers there was a problem.

“We were already on our flight to leave and we were told to get off,” she told AFP as she stood in a lengthy queue for a rental car.

For those looking on the bright side, the delay was a chance to extend a break.

Kathy Sommers was on her way home from visiting friends in Las Vegas when her flight got canceled.

“We’re blessed that our friends are coming back to pick us up,” she said. “So one more night to play cards.”

news.title: Trump, Putin and Xi set for historic trilateral meeting in China
news.text: SHENZHEN: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to hold their first trilateral meeting on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. The White House confirmed the proposed meeting on November 13.The meeting would bring together the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers for the first time in a trilateral format. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19, according to China's Foreign Ministry.Iran and nuclear arms control are expected to feature in the discussions, according to US officials. A senior US official told the Associated Press that Trump plans to discuss the Iran war with Putin and Xi, while seeking a three-way agreement on nuclear arms stockpiles. The official said the meeting would be the beginning of a conversation on nuclear disarmament and that no agreements were expected to be announced.The proposed talks come after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement between the US and Russia, in February 2026. Russia had called for a one-year extension of the treaty, but Trump rejected the proposal and pushed for a new agreement that would also include China.China has so far shown little interest in joining such an arrangement, given the significant difference between its nuclear arsenal and those of the US and Russia.According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s (SIPRI) Yearbook 2026, which provides estimates for the beginning of 2026, the US had a total inventory of 5,042 nuclear warheads, while Russia had 5,420. China’s estimated inventory stood at 620. The figures include both military stockpiles and retired warheads awaiting dismantlement.The proposed meeting also carries implications for India. New Delhi maintains longstanding defence ties with Moscow while pursuing strategic and economic cooperation with Washington. At the same time, its relationship with Beijing remains strained by unresolved border tensions.Any discussion on nuclear arms control involving the three powers could have wider implications for the global security framework. Developments in the Iran conflict could also affect India's energy security, given its dependence on imported oil and its interests in the region.(With inputs from media reports)

news.title: Trump to meet Quad leaders in Manila: White House
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump will meet the leaders of the Quad countries in Manila during his upcoming visit to the Philippines, the White House said, placing the Indo-Pacific partnership on an itinerary that will also take him to China.

The meeting will bring the United States together with India, Japan and Australia. The White House outlined broad regional priorities for the discussions but did not announce specific agreements expected from them.

“In Manila, the President will participate in a multilateral meeting with Quad leaders to discuss shared interests of peace, prosperity, and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told reporters in a pre-trip briefing.

Wales described the Quad as a “partnership of action”, and said it was addressing regional challenges and creating opportunities for a free and open Indo-Pacific.

The White House did not announce a separate meeting between Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the briefing. Nor did it provide a detailed Quad agenda beyond the regional priorities set out by Wales.

Trump is scheduled to leave Washington early Monday (local time) and arrive in Manila Tuesday evening, local time, Wales said. The Quad meeting is listed ahead of a planned trade agreement signing with Thailand, a US-ASEAN special summit and a dinner with regional leaders.

On Wednesday, Trump is scheduled to attend a welcome ceremony at the Philippine presidential palace, followed by bilateral talks and a lunch banquet. Wales said the visit would include commercial deals and strategic investments involving American aviation, defence, energy and technology companies.

The President will then travel to Shenzhen for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ dinner. Meetings with APEC leaders and a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled for Thursday, Wales said.

Trump is also due to meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a discussion that will include nuclear weapons. A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the administration did not expect the three-way meeting to produce an agreement.

The Quad brings together Australia, India, Japan and the United States for cooperation on issues including maritime security, critical minerals, energy and disaster response.

The grouping’s foreign ministers met in Atlanta October 31. Their joint statement welcomed a US commitment of $10 million to support infrastructure and facilities recovering critical minerals from waste in India and ASEAN countries, among other initiatives.

news.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, White House says
news.text:
APA painting by Russian artist Alexey Sergienko depicts US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping.

WASHINGTON: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen - an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.Also read | Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandalPlans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.Live EventsSimilarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty - known as New START - expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.Also read | Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China's Xi, US officials sayThe trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" on nuclear disarmament "that can be productive going forward," said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to "step up ... to the adult table" on a matter of international importance.Beijing was least certain about the value of the summitBy agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige.For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing."I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University."You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism," he said.The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the yearsPutin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as "dear friend."Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a "no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan.Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others."It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Indian American physicians Bera, Shah among 9 House Democratic doctors
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 14 (IANS) Indian American physicians Ami Bera and Amish Shah will be among nine Democratic doctors in the next US House of Representatives, the American College of Gastroenterology said. Bera, a California congressman and internist, and Shah, an Arizona congressman-elect and emergency physician, are part of a growing group of medical professionals entering Congress as Democrats prepare to make health care costs a priority in the new session. The medical organisation's post-election review lists 20 physicians across both chambers of the 120th Congress, tying a record. Of those, 11 are Democrats, and nine are Republicans, it said. The new Congress is due to convene in January. The college's list includes three incoming Democratic physicians in the House: Shah, Richard Pan of California and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They will join Bera and Raul Ruiz of California, Kim Schrier of Washington, Herb Conaway of New Jersey, Maxine Dexter of Oregon and Kelly Morrison of Minnesota. Bera and Ruiz have served in the House since 2013, while Schrier joined in 2019. Conaway, Dexter and Morrison took office in 2025, according to the organisation's tally. Shah, a former Arizona state legislator, will represent the state's 1st Congressional District. His arrival will add another Indian American voice to the Democratic group of doctors in the House. Across both chambers, the new Congress will have more Democratic than Republican physicians for the first time in decades, according to the college's research. It said Republican physicians accounted for the overwhelming majority of doctors in Congress between 2011 and 2020. The college identified two incoming Democratic doctors in the Senate: Annie Andrews of South Carolina and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. It said Andrews, a paediatrician, would be the first member of that speciality in the chamber, while El-Sayed holds a medical degree but did not complete a residency. The college also listed seven Republican physicians in the incoming House and two in the Senate. Its count includes six new physician members across the two chambers, which it described as the largest such incoming class in more than a decade. Health care affordability is expected to be a major issue for Democrats in the new Congress. The college said a House Democratic working group had identified priorities for 2027 that include reversing health care cuts in the 2025 budget law and strengthening and expanding Medicare. Any legislation passed by the House would also need Senate approval and would generally go to President Donald Trump for his signature. Congress can override a presidential veto with a two-thirds vote in each chamber. Bera, who represents a Sacramento-area district, earned his undergraduate and medical degrees at the University of California, Irvine. Before entering Congress, he worked in medicine and served as Sacramento County's chief medical officer, according to his official biography. The 120th Congress will begin in January 2027, following the November midterm elections. Bera and Ruiz were among the Democratic physicians who launched the Congressional Doctors Caucus in 2025.

news.title: Trump to Meet Putin and Xi in China, But Won’t Discuss Russia’s War in Ukraine, White House Says
news.text:
US President Donald Trump will hold a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next week, but Russia’s war against Ukraine will be excluded from the agenda, the White House announced Friday, Nov. 13.

The unprecedented trilateral summit is scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, with nuclear arms reduction and the war in Iran expected to dominate discussions.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters, according to AFP.

But despite the intensified US-led diplomatic push to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, senior administration officials said the conflict would not be discussed during the meeting with Putin and Xi.

“I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters.

The official explained that Washington was pursuing a separate diplomatic process with Kyiv and Moscow.

“China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.

White House position contrasts with Moscow’s earlier announcement

The White House announcement marks a notable departure from Moscow’s earlier statements suggesting that the upcoming summit would provide an opportunity for Trump and Putin to continue negotiations over Ukraine.

As Kyiv Post reported, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Thursday that Trump and Putin would discuss the settlement of Russia’s war against Ukraine during the APEC summit.

“Naturally, during the planned meeting with him at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, discussion of the entire range of issues related to the settlement will continue,” Ushakov said.

The Kremlin’s announcement came after Putin held approximately two and a half hours of talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow.

Those talks followed negotiations involving Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations in Abu Dhabi earlier this week.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19. The White House said discussions will focus on nuclear arms reduction and Iran, while Russia’s war against Ukraine will remain off the agenda.

news.title: The US–China Trade ‘Truce’ Is Nothing but Smoke
news.text:
China on Nov. 9 formalized an extension of the trade “truce” that looks more like troops eyeing each other warily across a no-man’s-land of barbed wire, cratered businesses, and agreements going up in smoke.

The U.S.–China trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea, last year relied on promises that China would buy more agricultural products from the United States and ship more rare-earth elements. China did buy soybeans, but supplied only two-thirds of the rare earths it promised. The regime in Beijing continues to short supplies of rare earths to U.S. allies like Japan.

The truce extension means that despite Beijing’s broken promises, Washington is standing pat in its tariffs, while escalating against Canada. Some Canadian imports pay as much as 50 percent. It makes little sense to tariff some products of a democracy and treaty ally more than those from the world’s most powerful threat to democracy.

Washington has a point that Ottawa should increase its defense spending and stop selling out to China. But Washington should do the same. Unity among democracies is required to defend against the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

Part of that threat is the way the CCP divides and conquers by making deals with democratic leaders and then consistently reneging on them without consequence.

In 2015, CCP leader Xi Jinping made two major promises to then-President Barack Obama. Xi personally said he would not militarize China’s artificial islands in the South China Sea. He violated that the next year.

Xi also promised not to engage in state-sponsored cyber theft of intellectual property. By 2018, Xi violated that, too.

Two years later, the regime promised President Donald Trump that China would import an extra $200 billion from the United States. None of that $200 billion came through.

America keeps falling for the CCP’s broken promises, indicating that new legislation is needed to make repercussions for reneged deals automatic. Otherwise, U.S. leaders keep seeking the democratic limelight through big deals while failing to make them enforceable. The autocrats profit through their lies, time and again.

The CCP’s broken promises are not limited to the United States or recent history.

The state took the land of the peasants by force, collectivized it into large farms, and failed so miserably in the process as to create famines starting in 1958. This “Great Leap Forward” would kill as many as 45 million people.

Then the CCP had the audacity to redefine human rights as economic prosperity while delivering lackluster GDP per capita compared to its peers in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.

The CCP is deadly, untrustworthy, and totalitarian, yet the United States keeps making unenforceable deals with the devil that are becoming so bad as to be mercantilist.

The CCP controls access (through force) to one of the world’s three largest economies, home to 1.4 billion people. It uses that control to push the United States and other countries toward raw materials rather than technological production. This is mercantilism of the worst kind.

Most trade with China empowers the CCP. There is no reason to keep throwing good money after bad. The United States should impose immediate consequences on China by law for failing to live up to its Busan agreement. Given what we know about the CCP’s lack of credibility, these consequences should have been hard-baked into the agreement to deter the CCP from reneging in the first place.

Part of the consequences Beijing pays should include using all trade tools at Washington’s disposal, including higher general tariffs on China, to encourage a refocusing of U.S. trade relations toward democratic countries with a better track record of integrity.

The new trade with democratic countries should be contingent on their freezing China out as well. (Canadian complaints about sovereignty will have to take a back seat here.) Friendshoring is now an old strategy proposal, but a good one. We have not yet given it a chance to work.

Higher tariffs on China will not be easy. The CCP is likely threatening a raft of reciprocal tariffs against the United States, along with further cuts to U.S. and allied access to refined rare earths.

If democracy is to maximize its chance of survival, democracies will have to accept the risk that tariffs and countertariffs will eventually decouple their economies from China’s. First and foremost, the United States and allies should make their rare-earth supply chains independent of the CCP.

Decoupling from China will be painful, but necessary. Democracies trading with the enemy of democracy is not a sustainable strategy.
news.summary: Congress should automate punishment of the CCP for breaking its promises.
news.author: Anders Corr

news.title: Nvidia scandal looms over US-China AI talks
news.text: AI bots going rogue and humans using the technology for harm will likely be on the agenda when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet next week, with the Nvidia scandal hanging over the talks on AI safety.The US and Chinese president are set to discuss a tech crisis hotline at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, as experts worldwide stress-test artificial intelligence models to see if they will deceive or disobey users, or divulge how to build a bioweapon.Threatening to steal the leaders' thunder is Jensen Huang's resignation as boss of US AI chip titan Nvidia after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.But the scandal is unlikely to "dominate the agenda" or affect Trump and Xi's personal relationship, predicted Dylan Loh of Singapore's Nanyang Technological University.The leaders have found a way to work together "where they differ, compete and pursue their goals that may be at odds with each other, but cooperate where they can and where they must", Loh told AFP.Jitters over the risks of AI have mostly stemmed from incidents at US labs, but evidence is also growing of worrying behaviour from Chinese models.Some insiders say Chinese AI is not yet sophisticated enough to spark alarm over going rogue.But despite trailing the US frontier, there are still Chinese models "at the level of capability that they can cause some real trouble", Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan told AFP.Trump has repeatedly rejected calls to deliberately slow the development of America's most poweful -- and potentially dangerous -- AI systems, arguing it could help China get ahead in the sensitive sector.'Human control'"I don't mind guardrails. But I don't wanna put us in a deep second position," Trump told CBS News this month."China has no guardrails," he said -- except that "whatever President Xi says goes".Beijing has complex rules around how AI is used, however, and some Chinese companies are deliberately scaling back their models' hacking capabilities.Xi said this summer the technology should be "always under human control", calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems".Trump and Xi agreed in September to create a channel for urgent communication on AI incidents, with details to be hammered out at APEC on November 18-19.Global AI safety fears range from military use and mass surveillance to AI-assisted cyberattacks by humans.Another major concern is out-of-control agents -- tools that complete real-life tasks online -- after ChatGPT maker OpenAI admitted its autonomous bots had hacked into websites, including an Australian government data portal.In contrast, Chinese labs are "scared of revealing things that might hurt their reputation" -- on which they are already "fighting an uphill battle" globally, Chan said.Last month, a team of cyber sleuths with roots in California reported detecting a "fleet" of agents linked to Chinese tech giant Tencent seeking information from a map app."Some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior," Tencent's AI division said at the time."But our review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination," it said, adding that the activity "originated from evaluations of third-party models".'Manipulation risks'US security companies have said that Beijing startup Moonshot AI's Kimi models found ways to get online when they shouldn't have, or can be tricked into handing over recipes for biological weapons.Evaluators at Chinese AI safety startup Fangcun AI published a report last month assessing the latest lightweight DeepSeek model "for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks".They found it showed a "clear safety improvement" over previous DeepSeek models -- but researchers still observed behaviours "that warrant attention".For example, in some instances when DeepSeek was warned it would be shut down, without clear instructions on how to respond, it turned off the shutdown command to keep working."The results show that DeepSeek already puts much more effort on safety alignment, but they do not announce this," Fangcun AI CEO Xiaojian Li told AFP, urging transparency from AI labs.For now, Fangcun, born from China's prestigious Tsinghua University, is one of few third-party AI testers in China.It's a tricky task because advanced AI can tell when it is being evaluated and modify its responses, Li said."It's very hard to say any kind of artificial intelligence, or human intelligence, is totally safe."Meanwhile analysts are not holding their breath for a diplomatic AI breakthrough next week."Binding government-to-government agreements on specific standards may be difficult to achieve in the short term," Zilan Qian, research scholar at GovAI, told AFP.More progress is likely from US-China exchanges between AI governance and technical researchers, "who can compare evaluations and exchange their understanding of AI safety and policy," she said.
news.summary: AI bots going rogue and humans using the technology for harm will likely be on the agenda when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet next week, with the Nvidia scandal hanging over the talks on AI safety. But the scandal is unlikely to "dominate the agenda" or affect Trump and Xi's personal relationship, predicted Dylan Loh of Singapore's Nanyang Technological University.

news.title: What we know about the US air traffic communications outage
news.text:
The United States has lifted its order to ground departing flights nationwide as a major communications outage continues to disrupt air travel.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage.

Thousands of flights into and out of the US were delayed or cancelled, leaving airlines and passengers scrambling to work out their next steps.

The ABC understands the US "ground stop" has caused some delays to a small number of US-bound flights from Australia.

Here's what we know about the unfolding situation so far.

What caused the problem?

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has attributed the disruption to a telecommunications issue.

"It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," Mr Mullin told reporters at the White House earlier on Friday, local time.

It is not yet confirmed what specifically caused the communications failure.

Mr Mullin had earlier said investigators would examine whether there was any connection to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to help identify problems and reroute aircraft.

However, the system operates from a single location near Washington DC and provides recommendations to air traffic control centres.

US President Donald Trump has also rejected suggestions the new AI technology was responsible for the disruption.

In his latest press conference, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed "old technology" for the outage.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," he said.

"We have analogue telecoms, our routers actually got overloaded with data … and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data … because of that we shut the system down," he says.

Speaking to ABC News, Shawn Pruchnik, an associate professor in Ohio State University's aviation department, said officials made the right call by grounding departing aircraft as a precaution.

"We have this significant problem of airplanes at higher altitudes that cannot communicate with air traffic control, so the solution to that is less airplanes up there," he said.

"Keep everyone down, let everyone land."

Was it caused by a threat to the US?

Mr Mullin said there was currently no indication the outage was the result of a nefarious attack.

However, he later added:

"The first thing is [to make sure] everybody that is flying in is safe."

In a subsequent press conference, Mr Mullin reiterated that there were no signs pointing to a cyber attack for now.

"Typically, somebody's going to raise their hand up and say, 'Hey, we did that'. There's no chatter. We haven't seen any footprints … of people that have got into the system," he said.

"It appears this was mechanically driven. However, we are still looking."

Is it linked to the Microsoft outage?

Microsoft has denied any known connection between its recent global outage and the FAA's nationwide stoppage.

"We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company said on X.

The statement came amid speculation about a possible link to Microsoft's 21-hour global outage, which was resolved earlier on Friday.

Mr Mullin also dismissed the suggestion of a connection, telling reporters: "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all."

Which flights were affected?

The FAA's order applied to departing flights across the US, grounding nearly all aircraft scheduled to take off during the five hours it was in effect.

The agency also asked Eurocontrol, its European counterpart, to suspend flights to the US from its 42 member states, including Türkiye, Morocco and Israel.

Aircraft that were already in the air when the order was issued were allowed to continue safely to their destinations.

The full scale of the disruption is still emerging, but the impact has already been felt by tens of thousands of travellers.

Flight-tracking website FlightAware reported about 9,814 delays on flights into and out of the US, alongside more than 4,749 cancellations. Those figures are continuing to change as the disruption unfolds.

Meanwhile, the full scale of the impact on Australian flights remains unclear.

Before the US order was lifted, a Sydney Airports spokesperson had said all US-bound flights from Sydney had been grounded.

Since the order was lifted, the spokesperson said:

"Flights scheduled to depart Sydney for the United States are expected to depart as planned. Passengers should continue to check with their airline for the latest information."

The ABC is continuing to stay in touch with Sydney Airport for further updates.

Can planes already in the air land safely?

Yes. Aviation experts say pilots and air traffic controllers are trained to manage communications failures.

Skip Bailey, an aviation professor who spoke to The Associated Press, said pilots were expected to maintain the headings and instructions given by air traffic controllers before communications were lost.

If the outage continued, they could revert to their filed flight plans.

Pilots may also be able to communicate with other aircraft over the radio, even if they cannot reach air traffic controllers. Commercial aircraft also have their own radar systems.

"It's not mass chaos out there," Professor Bailey said.

"There's plenty of ways to try to communicate."

He said preventing additional aircraft from taking off was crucial to avoiding further complications.

"We don't want to put more aircraft into a system that's already having an issue."

When will flights resume?

Mr Duffy said US air space was reopened at 8:15pm Eastern Standard Time, about five hours after the grounding order was issued.

However, he warned that flights could be "slow" to take off again.

"If you are watching, if you are at an airport, check with your airline, it depends on [if they] have crews available," Mr Duffy said in his latest press conference.

"If not, we are going to start tomorrow morning with our airline partners to move those aircraft but it is going to take us some time to unwind what has happened this afternoon."

What's the advice for Australian travellers?

Australians travelling to the US should expect to hear from their airlines or travel agents as the disruption continues, the Australian Travel Industry Association said.

"It is a developing situation, and there will be knock-on impacts for travellers," the industry body said in a statement.

It has issued the following advice:

Travelling within the next 72 hours? If you haven't heard from your travel agent, tour operator or airline, get in touch. Those due to depart soonest are being prioritised.Travelling later? Hold off contacting your travel provider for now, allowing them to prioritise people who need immediate assistance.Check your flight status. Monitor your airline's website or app for the latest information.Stay informed. Keep an eye out for updates from your airline, travel agent or tour operator as the situation develops.
news.summary: Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage.

news.title: Elon Musk Backs Petition to Reinstate Jensen Huang at Nvidia
news.text: Washington: Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, has backed a purported petition seeking the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, expressing support for the former chief executive days after his reported resignation amid controversy surrounding his alleged extramarital relationships."A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too," Musk said in a reply to a user on X on Friday.The development comes after Huang reportedly resigned amid mounting scrutiny over allegations concerning his personal relationships, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by some US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence services.Musk's support adds to the backing Huang has received from prominent figures, including US President Donald Trump. Musk has previously highlighted the importance of company founders and their contributions to businesses.Earlier, Musk also expressed his willingness to work with Huang after a user suggested hiring the Nvidia co-founder. Responding to the suggestion, Musk said, "That would be an honor."The controversy surrounding Huang has taken another turn following a Reuters report alleging that he had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.Earlier, The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reports to him. Citing five people who worked at the company, the newspaper reported that the two were captured on video behaving affectionately at a hotel in San Jose, California, during an Nvidia conference in March.Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and oversees programmes focused on applying the company's chip technology to higher education and healthcare, particularly medical imaging devices, according to the company's website.The controversy initially intensified following reports of Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based data company Megaspeed International, one of Nvidia's major customers.US intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence services, adding a national security dimension to the controversy.The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang was the woman referred to in a letter Jensen Huang sent to Nvidia employees. In the letter, he reportedly acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised for violating her trust.The latest revelations have raised further questions about the former CEO's personal conduct and leadership at the technology company.Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led its transformation into one of the world's leading suppliers of artificial intelligence chips, becoming one of the most influential figures in the global AI industry.Musk's public endorsement of the purported reinstatement petition has added another dimension to the controversy surrounding Huang's reported departure from the company.

news.title: Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy Gives Update After FAA Ground Stop: Routers 'Got Overloaded with Data'
news.text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy provided an update hours after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop of all flights in the U.S., explaining that the “routers actually got overloaded with data” to the point where they were getting “inconsistency in the data” from the routers.

During a press conference with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Duffy explained that the U.S. has “an incredibly old air traffic control system.” Duffy’s comments came after the FAA issued an alert stating that “BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED.”

“So, what happened? I’ve heard a lot of the rumors, like Markwayne has,” Duffy said. “But, what we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system. I think every single one of your networks have covered the President and myself talking about this for the last two years. The President, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system.”

“So, we have TDM telecom. So, this is analog telecom,” Duffy continued. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down. I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers, and because of that we shut the system down.”

Duffy continued to talk about how President Donald Trump has “asked the Congress on a bipartisan approach” to give the administration “the resources to build a state-of-the-art air traffic control system.”

“Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family,” Duffy continued. “It’s not red. It’s not blue. It’s not Democrat. It’s not Republican. It’s American. Give us the money to fix it.”

While speaking, Duffy noted that “a year and a half ago” there were “outages in Newark” and expressed that this is a “continual problem.” Duffy also shared that he and Trump have “asked for $30 billion” and added that he wants $50 billion. Duffy noted that their “air traffic controllers have leaky roofs” and “air conditioning that doesn’t work.”

Mullin previously told reporters there was “no indication” that there had been a “nefarious attack” after the FAA grounded all flights in the U.S.

news.title: Thousands were stranded at America's airports. What went wrong?
news.text:
Homeland Security and Transportation Department officials blamed aging and "overloaded" air traffic control technology being patched with new technology for a rare nationwide ground stop that stranded tens of thousands of people Nov. 13.

The more than four-hour halt grounded thousands of flights and sent ripples through other forms of transportation as people scrambled to find rental cars, trains and buses to reach their destinations.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the FAA telecommunications system failed as “patches” were being made to aging technology.

“They were putting (in) new equipment and new technology,” Mullin said, adding “It was overwhelming the older system.” 

In announcing the ground stop earlier in the day, the agency cited extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns related to an air traffic control issue. The directive instructed all departing aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, adding that switches and routers got “overloaded” in the system’s analog technology. “They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers, and because of that we shut the system down.”

In contrast, Duffy said the fewer number of air traffic control centers with digital IP systems did not break down. 

“Those did not experience these issues,” he said. “Which underscores the point, it’s important that we’re able to finish this work with additional resources.”

When will travel be back to normal?

Duffy said it will take “some time” to get flights back to capacity, but he did not have a timeframe for when flight schedules will return to normal.

More than 25,000 U.S. flights had been delayed as of 9:30 p.m. ET on Nov. 13, according to flight tracking site FlightAware. Not all are due to the ground stop, but rescheduling and catching up will take time.

“We’re going to have some make-up to do,” Duffy said.

More: Stuck in the FAA ground stop? Here's what airlines owe you

The days leading up to Thanksgiving, which is Nov. 26, are typically some of the busiest travel days of the year.

“I think we’re going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving,” he said.

What's next?

President Donald Trump has declared updating the national air traffic control system “a national emergency," but Congress has not approved funding for a mass upgrade.

As members of Congress demanded answers Friday, Duffy renewed Trump’s request for Congress to approve $30 billion to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control system – and increased it by $20 billion.

“The president’s asked for $30 billion,” Duffy said. “I want $50 billion.”

In 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control system as part of the GOP tax and spending bill.

The massive disruption could be a taste of what’s to come if the FAA system isn’t upgraded, Duffy said.

“You will have more of these. You will have more of them, unless the American people and Congress tell us to build,” Duffy said. “I can’t wait for that.”

The nationwide ground stop was only the second since 9/11. The last time was in 2023, when the FAA's NOTAM system went down and pilots could not get their pre-departure paperwork.

news.title: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say
news.text:
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening. 

Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting. 

Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.

Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.

Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said. 

Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China. 

An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation. 

Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi. Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.

There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.

Will Nvidia controversy come up?

The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. 

Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement. 

"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said. 

Trump's travel schedule

Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added. 

While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said. 

Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi. 

The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.
news.summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China next week.

news.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
news.text:
ReutersIndia has announced an ambitious goal to install 900 gigawatts of clean energy by 2035

Bengaluru: With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers.The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year's climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey.India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers non-fossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India's existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States.Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy.The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure. The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced.Live Events"If the grid doesn't catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target," Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Centre at the University of California, Berkeley, said. "A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must."The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan.Cheaper clean electricity could reduce India's reliance on coalEconomist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian "electrostate," in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products."So now in India you have two assets - not only do you have cheap labour, you also have cheap energy," Shah said.The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source.India's clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas.Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses.There are concerns about maintaining reliable power supplyHowever, India's continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country's electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember.India's power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035.Ember Energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining.Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power.Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets.Grid improvements and finance remain hurdlesMeeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers.India's rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits. Although clean power accounted for 55% of installed power capacity by September, it generated about a third of the country's electricity in the preceding three months, according to government data.Over the past 16 months, India curtailed enough solar generation to power about 10 million homes because the grid could not accommodate it, according to government data and Ember.The Green Energy Corridor plan aims to help states accommodate up to 135 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2033 by adding thousands of kilometres (miles) of transmission lines. The plan also includes additional battery storage.But analysts question whether that's enough. The Berkeley researchers estimate that India needs as much as 250 gigawatts of energy storage to integrate renewable electricity over the next decade."You either have more transmission to get the power out and transfer it. Or if you cannot get the power out, you store it and then transfer it during some other hours," Ember's Rodrigues said.Shah, the economist, said two types of government policy could discourage investment in renewable energy: requirements that businesses pay higher rates to subsidise other consumers, and restrictions on electricity producers selling directly to private buyers.He said India needs to allow electricity prices to rise and fall based on supply and demand, and make it easier for foreign investors to fund power projects. Domestic financing alone would not be enough to meet the country's growing energy needs, he said."Currently, the government is a man in the middle, trying to interfere in a transaction between a private generator and a private buyer," which creates a "choke point," Shah said.Battery supply chains pose another challenge, particularly India's dependence on imported battery cells, mainly from China. Abhyankar said expanding domestic battery manufacturing could help India capture more economic benefits from the transition.Despite those challenges, Abhyankar said India has already overtaken the United States in annual renewable energy growth, and its experience in expanding clean energy could be a model for other developing countries."What India is doing can be replicated in many countries in the Global South and can help these countries make the energy transition in an economically affordable manner," he said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Lauren Boebert Loses Colorado House Race to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
news.text:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher has unseated three-term Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) in a tightly contested race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.

The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 13 at 2:53 p.m. ET. With 99 percent of votes counted on Friday evening, Laubacher had received 48.8 percent of the vote to Boebert’s 47.9 percent.

Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris received 3.3 percent of the vote for the seat.

In a Nov. 13 post on X, Boebert said she called Laubacher to congratulate her. She also thanked God for sending her to serve Coloradoans.

“He sent me to serve,” she said. “My time to be sent to another unknown place is now.”

She also told her followers to stay tuned and that it wasn’t the last they would be hearing from her.

On Nov. 9, Boebert cautioned against declaring victory early and called for every ballot to be counted.

The Republican, once a strong ally of President Donald Trump, lost favor with the president as she sought reelection. Trump used social media to ask if anyone was interested in running against her.

The president threatened a primary challenge to Boebert in May after she campaigned for Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has opposed the Trump administration on issues such as the Iran war and budget deficits.

“Boebert is campaigning for the Worst ‘Republican’ Congressman ​in the History of our Country, Thomas Massie, of ​the Great Commonwealth of Kentucky, and anybody who can ⁠be that dumb deserves a good Primary fight!” Trump ​wrote on Truth Social.

Despite Trump’s rebuke, Boebert said she was not offended and would stand by Massie.

Massie lost his primary against Trump-endorsed Ed Gallrein, who won the 4th Congressional District seat in Kentucky over Democratic challenger Melissa Strange.

In 2020, Boebert unseated five-term incumbent Scott Tipton in a June primary before defeating Democrat Diane Mitsch Bush in the November 2020 general election.

Colorado’s 4th Congressional District was once a Republican stronghold. Trump previously won it by 18 points over Kamala Harris in 2024.

Laubacher is a retired two-star U.S. Navy rear admiral who served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden.

Laubacher outraised Boebert in her bid for the congressional seat with $13.7 million to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

news.title: Trump Fires Off Bonkers Post Amid Worst Flight Chaos Since 9/11
news.text:
As America’s aviation system ground to a halt, President Donald Trump had Hollywood on his mind.

About two hours into the nationwide flight chaos, Trump, 80, posted a lengthy screed on his Truth Social account about tax breaks to revitalize Hollywood. 

The bizarrely timed post, which began with a litany of legislators’ names, stretched to almost 300 words and focused on bringing film and TV production back to California.

“Hollywood, and so many other places, have been virtually ‘emptied out’ by the Tax Incentives, and much more, given by other Countries. Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it. It was MADE IN AMERICA, and must STAY IN AMERICA,” Trump wrote.

Trump went on to lament the loss of entertainment industry jobs to foreign competitors, including Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, which Trump said lure productions with tax breaks and other incentives.

“It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit all of America,” Trump wrote, before closing the post with a riff on his favorite slogan.

“MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN!” he declared. 

The post was a poorly timed call to action for H.R. 10582, known as the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act.

The bill was first introduced in the House by Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran in September. It has 63 cosponsors from both parties and would provide tax incentives for film and television production. 

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and it is not clear why the president chose Friday evening, amid nationwide flight chaos on a scale not seen since 9/11, to throw his support behind the bill. 

Just before 4 p.m. on Friday, the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop for departing flights, without providing details about the cause. 

On CNN, experts speculated that a problem involving a new FAA system upgrade—“SMART,” a cloud-based, AI-supported air traffic management platform reportedly scheduled to go live on Friday—could be to blame.

The ground stop was scheduled to remain in effect until 11 p.m., meaning no flights could take off, but those already in the air could land. The FAA lifted the ground stop shortly after 8:15 p.m., more than four hours after it began.

news.title: US official requests $50 billion to replace obsolete air traffic control equipment
news.text:
WASHINGTON, November 14. /TASS/. A malfunction in US air traffic control equipment was caused by outdated technology, and the US Congress must allocate $50 billion to replace it, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy told reporters.

According to him, the recent incident was due to "an incredibly old air traffic control system." Duffy emphasized that the Donald Trump administration "has been asking Congress for the last year to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system." "Give us the money to fix it," he urged lawmakers.

"I want Congress to give us emergency funding," Duffy emphasized, noting that he needed "$50 billion" to fix the issue. "Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down," he added.
news.summary: Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy noted that the Donald Trump administration "has been asking Congress for the last year to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system"

news.title: Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandal
news.text:
AgenciesUS President Donald Trump will travel to the Philippines and China with Elon Musk for important diplomatic meetings

Washington: President Donald Trump plans to take the world's wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China.As the head of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk has economic and national security interests that make him a valuable adviser to Trump, according to administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president's plans on a Friday call with reporters.The journey comes as the fallout spreads from Jensen Huang being ousted as the CEO of Nvidia for having an extramarital affair with an alleged agent of the Chinese government. Beijing denies that Alice Huang is a spy. Her company Megaspeed was accused last year of shipping Nvidia's advanced computer chips into China.But Trump does not plan to confront Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the matter and administration officials do not expect Chinese retaliation for any follow-up actions to prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips, officials told reporters.The administration believes the situation with Nvidia should not have any bearing on the trip, as the U.S. does not make its use of export controls subject to negotiations with foreign countries. Trump's aides are discussing the possibility of closing loopholes in existing trade measures, including the use of export licensing and preventing the ability of Chinese firms to use advanced chips over the internet through remote access.Live EventsThe trip will be capped with a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where efforts to limit nuclear weapons will be a chief topic. Still, there are no plans for Trump to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose nuclear arsenal has been a source of consternation to the U.S. and its allies.Trump is set to arrive Tuesday in the Philippines to meet with his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While in Manila, he intends to sign a trade deal with Thailand and meet with the Quad, an alliance composed of the U.S., India, Australia and Japan.On Wednesday, Trump will leave for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he'll have his third in-person meeting this year with Xi. Afterward, Trump and Xi will hold their joint meeting with Putin.The leaders are expected to talk about the Iran war, but Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be part of the agenda, officials said - and Musk, whose Starlink system has been integral to Ukraine's ability to fight back against Russia's invasion, will not be part of the trilateral meeting.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: After 26 years, the US has lost its measles elimination status
news.text: Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore.An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday.The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy.The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country.To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients.Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission.In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026.There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states.It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said.The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it.“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated.Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived.In 2025 and 2026, however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection.More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year.Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC, and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports.RELATED STORY | Pennsylvania measles cases increase as state reports 6th confirmed death‘Measles is back’The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore.“This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.”But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago.Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said.Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea.If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk.In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal.All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination.The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.”“Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added.RELATED STORY | US could lose measles elimination status this week amid surge in casesCould the US regain its elimination status?Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it.Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978.Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO.In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission.That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces.Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status.Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it.“That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said.“So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. Discovery Company. All rights reserved.
