news.title: Trump To Meet Putin, Xi Next Week: Nuclear Arms, Iran War On Agenda; No Talks On Ukraine
news.text:
US President Donald Trump will raise the issue of nuclear arms reduction during an unprecedented meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next week, the White House said on Friday. The three leaders are expected to meet on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen.
White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Trump believes the proliferation of nuclear weapons poses a serious danger and wants to discuss reducing global nuclear stockpiles. The meeting will be part of Trump's four-day Asian tour, which begins on Monday and also includes a visit to the Philippines.
However, the US push to make nuclear disarmament a central topic has created some discomfort in Beijing, which is hosting a summit focused primarily on trade and commerce. China has repeatedly resisted attempts by Washington and Moscow to bring it into nuclear arms negotiations, citing the significant difference between its arsenal and those of the two countries.
Trump Wants China At The Table For Nuclear Arms Discussions
A senior Trump administration official said Washington was not expecting an agreement on nuclear arms reduction during the meeting. However, the administration hopes the discussion will mark the beginning of a broader conversation involving all three countries.
"This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it's time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults' table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official told reporters.
The official added that Washington viewed the meeting as an opportunity to initiate discussions that could eventually become productive. However, it remains unclear whether either Beijing or Moscow intends to engage with Trump on nuclear arms reductions.
China has maintained for years that direct negotiations with Washington over its nuclear programme are inappropriate, arguing that the US and Russia should first hold discussions because they possess significantly larger nuclear arsenals.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Russia has the world's largest stockpile of stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which governed nuclear arms limits between Washington and Moscow, expired this year.
Iran War On Agenda, Ukraine Unlikely To Be Discussed
Apart from nuclear disarmament, Trump is also expected to raise the US-Israeli war against Iran during his meeting with Putin and Xi. However, a senior administration official said the US President was unlikely to bring up Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.
Trump is also not expected to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin or discuss Ukraine's access to satellite communications services provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Musk is accompanying Trump on his China visit but will not be present during the meeting between the three leaders.
Explaining why Ukraine was unlikely to feature in the discussions, the US official said Washington had held several recent meetings with Moscow, while China was not part of that diplomatic engagement.
The official said it therefore did not appear appropriate to bring the Ukraine issue into the trilateral meeting.
Meanwhile, Trump is not expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his Asian tour, the administration official added.

news.title: US could spy on Germany through Tesla cars – regional intelligence chief
news.text:
Tesla vehicles could pose an espionage risk, Stephan Kramer, the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency (BfV) in the state of Thuringia, has warned. His remarks come as German officials call for restrictions on parking internet-connected cars near sensitive government and military facilities.

Tesla is an American company led by Elon Musk, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The electric carmaker operates a major factory near Berlin, making it one of the few foreign automakers with a significant manufacturing presence in Germany.

Kramer was commenting on the Bundeswehr’s decision to restrict access by internet-connected vehicles to sensitive areas of military bases. The measures apply regardless of manufacturer, including Tesla.

“We should not assume that friends do not spy on one another,” Kramer told Handelsblatt on Friday. “The same security standards should apply to Tesla and all other manufacturers.”

According to the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), Germany’s digital security watchdog, most new vehicles sold in the country have the technical capability to collect information, including location data, camera footage and sensor readings, and transmit it to manufacturers’ back-end systems.

There is no specific evidence so far that such data has been used for espionage, Handelsblatt reported. According to the BSI, customers are often unaware of exactly what data their vehicles generate and transmit.

“The cameras and location-tracking systems in [internet-connected] cars capture sensitive information,” Kramer warned. “At Bundeswehr facilities, that includes information about military installations, operational procedures and personnel,” he said, describing the restrictions as “strongly advisable and therefore proportionate.”

The intelligence chief called for similar restrictions in “particularly sensitive areas of government buildings, police facilities, intelligence agencies and other security-relevant institutions,” including designated parking zones or access limitations.

Kramer also advised civil servants and public employees against discussing confidential matters inside internet-connected vehicles.

His concerns were echoed by several MPs, including Marc Henrichmann of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Johannes Schaetzl, a digital policy spokesman for the Social Democratic Party’s parliamentary group.

“We must not be naive: Espionage today is no longer carried out solely by agents, but also through technology that we ourselves bring onto our premises,” Henrichmann told Handelsblatt.

Schaetzl expressed particular concern about vehicles produced by Chinese automaker BYD, which he described as “black boxes.” “We do not know exactly what data is collected or who has access to it,” he said.

Last month, Tesla reported delivering more vehicles globally than Mercedes-Benz’s passenger-car division in the third quarter of 2026. The German automaker has faced pressure from US import tariffs and growing competition in China, where domestic manufacturers such as BYD and Xiaomi are challenging established brands.
news.summary:
A German regional spy chief has warned that Tesla cars could pose an espionage risk, urging restrictions near military and government sites

news.title: Trump plans nuclear talks with Xi and Putin
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 14 (IANS) US President Donald Trump plans to discuss reducing nuclear weapons with the leaders of China and Russia during an Asia visit next week, but US officials do not expect the three-way meeting to produce an agreement. The meeting will conclude Trump's visit to China, White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales said during a briefing on his planned trip to the Philippines and China. A senior US official described the planned talks as the beginning of a conversation about reducing nuclear arsenals, rather than negotiations expected to yield an immediate pact. "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said on condition of anonymity. Trump intends to discuss Iran during the meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Ukraine is not expected to be on the agenda, the official said. Discussions with Russia about Ukraine are proceeding separately. No bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled, although they will attend other events together, the official added. The nuclear discussions form part of an itinerary combining regional diplomacy with efforts to implement existing trade arrangements. Wales said Trump would leave Washington early Monday and arrive in Manila on Tuesday evening, local time. In the Philippines, he is scheduled to meet Quad leaders, sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a US-ASEAN special summit. A state welcome ceremony, a bilateral meeting with the Philippine president and a banquet are planned for Wednesday. Trump will then travel to Shenzhen for an APEC leaders' dinner. Meetings with APEC leaders and a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi are scheduled for Thursday, Wales said. On trade, a senior US official said discussions with China would focus on implementing existing arrangements rather than announcing a new tariff agreement. The official said US Trade Representative and Treasury officials had met Chinese counterparts through the Board of Trade earlier that day. Their discussions covered potential tariff changes and non-tariff barriers that could undermine the value of an agreement. Washington remains dissatisfied with the pace and volume of Chinese shipments of rare earths and related products, the official said. That concern was part of the reason an arrangement referred to as the Busan agreement received a two-month extension rather than six months. Trump is expected to raise the issue with Xi, the official said. Any tariff changes would require separate legal procedures, including consideration of US statutory requirements and a possible notice-and-comment period, the official said. No announcement connected to the Board of Trade was expected during the leaders' meeting. US officials also said American export controls were national security matters and were not being negotiated with China. Measures under consideration included extending licensing requirements to other countries to address alleged chip smuggling and examining restrictions on remote access. Those measures remain under consideration, rather than announced policy changes. Elon Musk is expected to accompany Trump for portions of the China visit, an official said, but will not participate in the bilateral meeting with Xi or the three-way talks with Xi and Putin. Those meetings will involve officials only. The White House said the September meeting between Trump and Xi advanced work on bilateral boards of trade and investment. APEC provides a forum for economic engagement across the Asia-Pacific. Wales said the administration sees its meetings as an opportunity to expand markets for American exports and advance its trade, energy and growth priorities.

news.title: Live updates: Nationwide ground stop will be lifted shortly, source says
news.text:
BREAKING: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication ” that anything “nefarious” was behind the ground stop, but blamed a telecommunications outage.

Shortly before the ground stop was lifted, JetBlue tonight announced it was canceling the rest of the night’s flights, with the exception of Europe-bound ones from JFK and Boston.

“We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations,” the airline said in a statement shortly after 8 p.m. ET.

“Safety remains our top priority, and we are working closely with the FAA as we monitor the situation,” it said.

Duffy says he wants $50 billion to improve the nation’s air traffic control system.

“Let’s not do a patchwork fix to a system that’s critical for every single family,” Duffy said during tonight’s White House briefing.

He said President Trump has asked Congress for $30 billion.

Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported. The request is for an additional $30 billion.

Duffy pointed to previous air traffic control problems, including outages in Newark that disrupted flights.

“This is a continual problem that we have, and it should be fixed,” Duffy said.

Transportation Secretary Duffy said tonight that switches in the air traffic control system became overloaded with data.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said at a briefing at the White House.

“We have TDM telecoms, so this is analog telecom,” Duffy said.”Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data.”

He said the routers “started to give us inconsistency in the data.”

Duffy said new switches worked, but it was the old hardware that went down. He called on Congress to fund improvements to the air traffic control system. He said President Donald Trump has requested the money from Congress for improvements.

The ground stop was sparked after “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country,” Secretary Duffy said.

TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center.

“We have procedures for this,” Duffy said at a news conference tonight.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy listens at a White House briefing tonight, lifting the ground stop. Alex Wong / Getty

“We didn’t lose all telecom, we didn’t lose all radar,” Duffy said. “But that instability, because of an abundance of caution and making sure we keep the American public safe, we did the ground stop.”

There were around 3,500 planes in the air when the ground stop was called at 3:36 p.m. Duffy said that last time he checked, there were around 400 in the airspace.

DHS Secretary Mullin says that there is no sign of a cyberattack in today’s ground stoppage.

“So far what we’ve seen there is no cyberattack. We’re still working through that process,” he said. “Our teams are working through that process.”

He said that things were progressing “in the right direction.”

Mullin said the public was never in any danger and the ground stop was out of an abundance of caution.

32m ago / 8:36 PM ESTThe national ground stop has been liftedThe FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop, more than five hours after the initial public alert.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the airspace opened at 8:15 this evening.

The national FAA ground stop will be lifted imminently, a source familiar with the matter tells NBC News.

Orlando International Airport on Friday. Finn Gomez / Getty

However, resolving the impact will likely take time given many airline crews and planes are out of place, and considering pilot and flight attendant max duty time.

Shivani Hawkins had just landed in Los Angeles from the Bay Area when she learned about the nationwide ground stop.

She was traveling with her two young children and arrived for a flight tonight to Australia.

“We don’t have any idea what’s happening with our flight for the next six hours,” she said.

Shivani said the airline gave her family $30 food vouchers each, unprompted. “We’re just hanging out in the LAX area because Friday rush hour traffic has been brutal.”

Most days this week saw about 100 flight cancelations into and out of the U.S. — so far today, upwards of 5,300 flights have been canceled.

The Association of Organ Procurement Organizations, a national nonprofit that represents the U.S. organ donation community, said it is closely monitoring the ground stop.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Friday. Kamil Krzaczynski / AFP via Getty

The group said when a flight is disrupted, organ procurement organizations (OPO) work to find safe alternatives, including ground transportation.

The association said in a statement it works “around the clock” to “give every donated organ the best possible chance to save a life.”

“Hearts and lungs are among the most time-sensitive organs to transport. If a delay threatens an organ’s viability, the OPO shares the updated arrival estimate with the receiving transplant team, which uses its clinical judgment to determine whether the transplant can safely proceed,” Allison Erickson, the AOPO president, said.

“We hope the ground stop is resolved soon for everyone affected.”

Gillian Horn and her fiancé were on a Delta flight at John F. Kennedy International Airport, bound for a long-planned family trip to Morocco, when the pilot announced the national ground stop over the speakers this afternoon.

“It was obviously met by a huge chorus of groans. Everyone was kind of like, ‘No way!’” she told NBC News.

The couple already had a nightmare two days of travel as their original flight yesterday was canceled due to weather.

Today, they arrived at the airport around 2 p.m. for their 4 p.m. flight to Atlanta, where they would continue on to Marrakesh, when the ground stop was announced and they had to deplane.

The couple scrambled to rebook flights and decided to book one out of the U.S. in hopes of avoiding the ground stop to make it to Morocco. In total, they’ve been rebooked six times since yesterday.

She described Terminal 4 as packed, the Delta help desk line “astronomically long,” and many passengers leaving altogether.

Horn said around 6 p.m. she observed that flights to Europe were still planning to depart.

“We were sitting at a random gate, and it was at Catania, Italy. Out of the blue around 6 p.m. they go whoever to Catania, this flight is going to board in an hour,” she said. “There were claps, actual cheering and claps from the section.”

That inspired her and her fiancé to wait it out. Their flight to Paris was originally set to depart at 7 p.m. but got delayed twice to 9 p.m. She’s hopeful to board soon.

“It could be worse,” she said. “If we were stuck on the tarmac. Could be worse if we weren’t together. … At the end of the day, it’s fine. We want to get there safely. But we want to get there.”

The last time the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, after files in a system critical for pilots were accidentally deleted.

The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

The system that was damaged was NOTAM, or Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to potential dangers.

There was no evidence of a cyberattack, the Federal Aviation Administration said at the time. Instead, the department blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases.

The FAA said it made the necessary repairs to the system and had taken steps to make it more resilient.

President Donald Trump is getting constant updates on the situation with the nationwide ground stop, according to a senior White House official.

The FAA ordered the ground stop this afternoon, and it will run through at least 11 tonight.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”

There have been more than 10,00 U.S. flights delayed and over 4,000 cancellations today amid an extremely rare nationwide ground stop, according to a tracking website.

Denver International Airport on Friday. J. David Ake / Getty

At 7:30 tonight, FlightAware showed 10,079 U.S.-related delays and 4,238 U.S.-related cancelations.

Those numbers are far higher than in previous days. Yesterday, there were around 6,800 U.S.-related delays and 1,024 U.S.-related cancellations, according to the site.

Wednesday only had 3,424 delays and 99 cancellations in the U.S., it said.

Travelers have formed a long line at Chicago O’Hare International Airport’s baggage services desk. Among their questions: Where is their luggage? When will they get it?

2h ago / 7:18 PM ESTSpaceX allowed to launch rocket despite ground stop SpaceX was able to launch a rocket during the ground stop because the agency already had flight prohibitions around the launch site before the national ground stop was initiated.

“The FAA had already cleared airplanes around it, so it gave a nice path all the way up into space,” Jeff Guzzetti, an aviation safety expert, said. “All of that airspace above Texas and through the trajectory of the rocket was already cleared. There were already flight prohibitions in place.”

Guzzetti previously worked for the FAA and was involved in rocket launch preparations for the agency.

SpaceX launched the 15th uncrewed flight of its Starship rocket with the hopes that it would be the first round-trip rocket voyage back to the spot where it left Earth.

The launch took place in Texas just a few minutes after its opening window and the Starship entered orbit around the Earth just after 5 p.m. local time.

However, the company abandoned plans to return the rocket’s booster and collect it at the launchpad. Instead, the booster splashed down into the Gulf of Mexico after the company aborted the maneuver. SpaceX hopes to retrieve the upper stage of the rocket tomorrow after it orbits Earth about 14 times and returns to Earth.

An outage that affected millions of Microsoft customers around the world does not appear to be linked to the ground stop, the company said.

“Microsoft has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the recent service disruption,” a spokesperson said.

Danielle Curry heard about the nationwide ground stop on her way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport but still went to inquire about her flight.

“They don’t know if the flights are going to even go today, so they let me change it to tomorrow,” she said.

“I just wanted to get home,” she said. “But my aunt lives here, so I’m going back to my aunt’s house, so I’m lucky compared to most.”

But the uncertainty about the cause of the extraordinary ground stoppage, coupled with world events, left Curry uneasy.

“It’s a little scary, like, is it cyberattack? Like, what is actually happening?” she said.

Officials have said that there were no initial indications of a cyberattack, but that a cause for the telecommunication outage had not yet been determined.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time for them to travel to their games this weekend.

Most college football teams playing tomorrow travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, eighth-ranked Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games.

Meanwhile, the Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly today for games on Saturday. They had just boarded the team plane in New Orleans after playing the Pelicans earlier this week when their flight to Memphis was halted in place.

There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL tomorrow. And while the Panthers made it to St. Louis for their game before the stoppage began, the Sharks were among those that were left waiting to leave for their game in Utah.

The FAA did not provide a timeline for restarting flights, leaving sporting events taking place beyond tomorrow in limbo. That includes most of the Week 10 schedule in the NFL along with numerous college sporting events.

The National Weather Service said its radars are fully operational and working normally.

“Outdated content from isolated webpages stating otherwise has been circulating, but NWS radars are operating normally,” the agency said.

NBC News’ weather unit confirmed that a page on the agency’s site associated with public-facing radar data was down, but the site is now operational and all radar sites across sites across the U.S. were working.

FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, is among the parcel delivery services that are monitoring the ground stop, saying customers can track the status of their shipments through the company’s website.

“We are prepared to activate contingency plans to minimize service disruptions and will resume normal flight operations as soon as the FAA permits,” said Shannon Davis, a spokesperson for FedEx.

The FAA’s ground stop applies to all departing flights at U.S. airports and therefore affects cargo and package shipping operations that rely on air transport.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

FedEx has nearly 700 aircraft that operate around the globe, shipping an average of 17 million packages and 20 million pounds of freight daily, according to the company’s website. Most of those shipments are made in the U.S.

Gerardo Lopez was hoping to escape Chicago for sunny San Diego but was one of the travelers whose plans have been put on ice by the nationwide ground stoppage.

“It’s my only trip this year, so yes, it’s frustrating,” he told NBC Chicago at Chicago Midway International Airport. “I don’t get too much vacation.”

“I just wish they’d get their act together soon, so we can get out of here,” he said. “If not, I’ve got to head back home.”

We are more than three hours into the nationwide ground stop, which is an extremely rare occurrence.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Even though it’s a rail service, Amtrak said air travel issues are creating frustrations for its passengers.

“We’re currently experiencing higher-than-normal call volumes due to ongoing airline issues,” it said on social media.

Sierra Gould was on the last leg of a flight from Denver to her home in Corpus Christi, Texas, when the connecting flight from Houston was stuck on the ground by the national flight stoppage.

“Trying to remain calm, because panicking isn’t going to do any thing,” she said at Houston International Airport.

She hoped her flight would still happen, but wasn’t optimistic.

“I think I’m going to have someone drive out here and pick me up and go home,” Gould said. “Thank God I’m only three hours away.”

But a big concern is her luggage, because it was to be part of the connecting flight.

There’s a general sense of confusion among passengers at Denver International Airport amid a lack of information.

Very few travelers seem to grasp the big picture — that all outgoing planes across the nation have been grounded — and many airport TVs are broadcasting sports.

People in lines to rebook flights are seemingly unaware of the scale of the travel headache that’s unfolding across the U.S. There are big crowds and long lines for everything because people are stuck at the airport and aren’t leaving as usual.

Many people are calling their families and customer service to seek info and updates. The lines for food are growing longer and seating is getting harder to come by.

San Francisco International Airport said minutes ago that Pacific-bound flights have been cleared to leave, including to Hawaii and Asia.

It said that the clearance occurred at 3 p.m. local time (6 p.m. ET).

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.

“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, said its software didn’t cause today’s nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

The startup, which is based in Boston, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

3h ago / 6:09 PM ESTRedundancies in place so pilots can still receive information to safely land, aviation expert saysThere are multiple layers of communications for air traffic, and aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said that it’s the high-altitude control centers that are experiencing the outage today.

Pilots are trained to handle radio outages such as this and there are other means to relay information to them to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing, he said.

“There are redundancies in place so pilots can get this information and a lot of times the information can be communicated digitally on a screen in the cockpit,” he said.

“When you’re flying in high altitude in a cruise flight, you’re talking to an air route traffic control center that’s run by the FAA and that’s the one that’s having the problem,” Guzzetti said.

“Then they will hand you off to an approach controller that’s near a major city. You talk to the approach controller, which is a mid-level altitude, as you are making your descent to the airport, and then that controller hands you off one last time to the local controller, who’s at the control tower.”

At this early stage of the investigation into today’s communications outage, there is no indication that the incident was caused by malicious activity, multiple officials from multiple agencies involved tell NBC News.

They say they haven’t seen any evidence of the type of activity normally associated with a cyberattack.

A passenger sits next to the departure board at Miami International Airport. Joe Raedle / Getty

But the officials cautioned that it is early in the investigation and that the findings change as they continue to dig into the problem.

Three senior officials said there’s nothing that indicates a connection between today’s FAA incident and Microsoft’s widespread outage.

Today’s nationwide ground stop comes soon after the FAA implemented changes to the air traffic control system that it said would add the use of AI. It’s not clear, though, if the two are related.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy unveiled the system — known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART — in September, saying it “centralizes 200 data streams” into one platform. The benefits would include fewer delays and cancellations, he said.

The SMART platform drew skepticism from the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which said in a statement in September that it was not involved in the design, testing or implementation of the system. Democratic lawmakers also pushed back, asking the FAA in a letter Oct. 9 to pause the changes.

But after testing the system at airports in the Washington area, the FAA said this week that the platform was active nationwide and would use AI to help inform routing and schedule recommendations, according to reports in Flying magazine and Ars Technica.

“Using AI, SMART analyzes airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur,” the FAA says in a description of the program.

Planes are parked at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. John Locher / AP

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked by a reporter outside the White House about a possible connection between AI and the ground stop. He responded: “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We’re going through that process, and we’re going to find out what happened.”

A Republican leadership aide told NBC News early this evening that senior members have not yet received a briefing from administration officials on the nationwide ground stop.

Separately, a senior lawmaker told NBC News that they have gotten no information. When they inquired with officials, the lawmaker says they were told there is no information to share at this point.

The FAA blamed today’s ground stop on a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage — out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” it said on X.

“Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” it said.

Delta Airlines planes are seen at LaGuardia Airport in New York, today. Ryan Murphy / AP

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said that today’s outage is “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti, who said he doesn’t know the cause of the outage, stressed that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

He added that the situation is moving from a safety issue to a massive logistics problem.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is still communication with planes despite the ground stop.

“My understanding is that we can still communicate,” Mullin said this afternoon. “It’s just that it’s at different levels and clarity that we can get to.”

“But there’s redundancy in most communications,” he said. “So, as you can see, there’s still planes landing, and so there’s still communications going on.”

With all departing flights grounded, some airports are beginning to run out of space for jets.

A source with knowledge of the situation told NBC News that Reagan National Airport is at capacity and that Chicago O’Hare is nearing capacity, meaning there is no place for planes to park and that some of the planes may have to divert to other airports.

4h ago / 5:31 PM ESTSec. Mullin says FAA ground stop was caused by 'telecommunication outage'01:51Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters the nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration was the result of a telecommunication outage. He also assured that the issue was not the result of some form of attack or hack.

Deveren Werne was in Indianapolis headed to Chicago this afternoon on an American Airlines flight when the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now our plane is heading back to the terminal so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin at the White House. Alex Brandon / AP

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication as of yet” that there was anything “nefarious” that caused the ground stop. He said it was the result of a telecommunications outage “as of now.”

Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed and they “are not ruling out anything at this point” in terms of what caused the communications issue. He said those currently on flights have no reason for concern.

“We are assured that everybody is safe,” he said, adding that it was unprecedented.

A flight board showing delayed flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, today in Arlington, Va. Tom Brenner / AP

Planes across the country were grounded and not allowed to take off this afternoon after a “ground stop” was issued.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the ground stop at 4:16 p.m. today on X.

He said the Federal Aviation Administration “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

The order means flights are prevented from taking off.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” Duffy said. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”
news.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication ” that anything “nefarious” was behind the ground stop, but blamed a telecommunications outage.Ground stop will be lifted soon, source saysPassengers' refrain: We don’t have any idea what’s happening

news.title: Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China's Xi, US officials say
news.text:
ReutersDonald Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping next week during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in China

The meeting will come just days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, capping a spectacular fall from the chip industry's heights.Though semiconductors have been a major flash point in US-China relations, the US president is not expected to raise the latest issue with Xi for now, the officials said,"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the US, it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," one senior administration official told reporters.A second US official added: "I don't expect the president to raise it, the Alice Huang issue."Live EventsThe officials were responding to a reporter's question about whether Trump would raise the allegations involving Alice Huang with Xi.On Tuesday, the independent members of Nvidia's board said they hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation after the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported on Jensen Huang's relations with the businesswoman, Alice Huang, as well as US authorities' suspicions that she was spying for China.Beijing has denied she is a spy. Alice Huang could not be reached. Reuters has not independently verified whether Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government. news.title: Jensen Huang Scandal Puts Spotlight on National Security Concerns Over Nvidia’s AI Chips
news.text:
As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the global economy, it can be argued that no company has contributed to it more than Nvidia.

CEO Jensen Huang has long been considered one of the world’s leading voices on AI.

But his extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has potential implications for the broader economy, financial markets, and possibly national security.

From a struggling graphics-chip startup founded in a Denny’s booth over three decades ago to a global juggernaut with a roughly $4 trillion market cap, Nvidia has moved to the center of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

After years of burning through cash and making bets on graphics hardware, Nvidia reached a pivotal moment in 1999 when it introduced the first Graphics Processing Unit, or GPU.

That same year, Nvidia made its Wall Street debut and garnered access to a new pool of capital.

By the 2000s, Nvidia became integral to PC gaming.

After raising $42 million from its initial public offering, the company used the cash to fund the production of its revolutionary GeForce 256, which provided video game developers and gamers a notable leap in PC 3D gaming performance.

A key moment occurred in 2006 with the launch of Compute Unified Device Architecture, better known as CUDA, a software platform that became crucial for tasks beyond graphics rendering. Rather than merely drawing video game images, Nvidia’s GPUs performed a massive number of calculations simultaneously for artificial intelligence, machine learning, and scientific simulations.

This eventually laid the groundwork for the AI boom.

Six years later, researchers discovered that Nvidia’s chips were suitable for training AI models.

By the time the AI boom took off with the launch of ChatGPT, Nvidia’s chips had become indispensable to the AI ecosystem, powering everything from cloud computing and data centers to autonomous vehicles.

As Nvidia’s chips became essential to the global AI boom, the company found itself caught between commercial demand and national-security concerns.

Beyond commercial products, its lineup of chips—Blackwell and Hopper, for example—could provide the computing power needed to train and run advanced AI systems. Governments worldwide view AI as not only a technology to grow economies, but also as a cyber, intelligence, and military tool.

In other words, while Nvidia’s chips can help generate high-quality AI videos of Will Smith eating spaghetti, they can also support intelligence analysis and surveillance systems.

The United States has treated AI as the key to maintaining national security as well as a technological edge over geopolitical rivals like China. As a result, Washington has introduced export controls to achieve its dual objective: restrict China’s access to its powerful computing technology and maintain U.S. dominance in what has fast become an AI arms race.

The Biden administration’s 2022 export controls sought to curb China’s access to advanced AI semiconductors, placing Nvidia’s industry-leading products under heightened scrutiny.

U.S. officials later investigated whether Megaspeed—the Singapore-based firm connected to the affair that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation—helped facilitate the transfer of restricted processors to China. The probe also highlighted the use of Singapore-based entities by Chinese firms seeking continued access to foreign markets and sensitive technologies.

Lawmakers are now pressing ahead with legislation and are expected to include bills in the annual defense authorization act.

“I think we have all the authorities that we need,“ Bessent told CNBC’s ”Squawk Box” on Nov. 13. “They just need to be implemented.”

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, built a career that included journalism, finance, and private equity before entering the technology sector.

She moved into private equity in 2015 and had earlier claimed work experience with Hunan Television, reported the publication.

Her path eventually led to the artificial intelligence industry.

In 2023, Alice Huang became involved with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud-computing and data-center company that built business relationships within Nvidia’s AI ecosystem. Other reports suggest she regularly attended industry events with Nvidia executives and customers.

Through Megaspeed’s role as a Nvidia partner, she became connected to the fast-growing market for AI infrastructure and advanced semiconductor technology.

Citing unnamed intelligence officials, various media outlets reported that Alice Huang had ties to China’s Ministry of State Security, allegations that Beijing has denied.

What’s next for Nvidia is unclear, but President Donald Trump has floated Tim Cook as the former CEO’s replacement, and prediction markets are betting on Ian Buck.

No matter who is selected, Nvidia’s vision will remain intact, says Nancy Tengler, CEO and CIO at Laffer Tengler Investments.

“It is possible to replace an iconic CEO with a different kind of CEO,” Tengler said in a note emailed to The Epoch Times.

While some worry that Jensen Huang’s ousting could affect the broader AI boom, many market watchers say the fundamentals remain solid.

“As for the broader AI trade, we would view this primarily as a Nvidia-specific leadership issue rather than a fundamental change in the long-term AI investment thesis,” Ken Mahoney, president and CEO at Mahoney Asset Management, told The Epoch Times in an emailed note.

For now, this is a bumpy path for one of the world’s wealthiest companies.
news.summary: The CEO's admission of infidelity has sparked worries about the broader economy, financial markets, and possibly national security.

news.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: I'm told control over transfers was key to Mauricio Pochettino taking Man United job. It seems they finally have a manager bullish enough to hold Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Jason Wilcox to account
news.text:
It only happened once. But if you search for it, there is footage. The date was February 23, 2000 and the place was the old Wembley Stadium. England 0-0 Argentina, the kind of friendly best forgotten, except for a single line of trivia.

Of all the games played by Jason Wilcox and Mauricio Pochettino, this was the sole example of them sharing a pitch. Wilcox was given the full 90 at a point when Kevin Keegan was low on options for the left wing and Pochettino came on with 35 minutes on the clock and kicked a few people.

He was good at kicking people, Pochettino. He flattened Paul Scholes once, then he nudged over David Beckham and twice he got stuck into Emile Heskey. But Wilcox was in a safe zone on the other side of the field that night. While Pochettino indulged his hobby, Wilcox kept out of harm’s way.

We might ask at this juncture if either of them ever changed their spots. But it’s more interesting to ponder what comes next, now they have been pitched together again at Manchester United.

United needed a big bull to replace Michael Carrick and they have got one. Wilcox’s preference? Well, United’s director of hopeless football quite fancied Eddie Howe, according to the whispers, and Howe is far from a shrinking violet, but he’s not Pochettino. And Pochettino certainly isn’t Carrick.

Pochettino won’t drive to work for three days straight while knowing his race is run. And he won’t have the same patience for incompetence from those below or above.

With any luck, United knew this when they reached an agreement that was a decade in the making. If they did, it would demonstrate some self-awareness at last, because United have badly needed the right blend of bruiser and diplomat in that seat. 

They have cried out for someone who isn’t too nice, too loyal, too whiny or too undermined by their own shortcomings to have the kind of rucks that are needed for change. By that logic, United may have invited their own worst enemy to dinner, or their best chance of a solution.

There have been few managerial appointments in recent years as inherently fascinating at this one. That instinct is partly driven by the thought it has all arrived a touch late – when United favoured Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to replace Jose Mourinho, it was a sliding-door moment for all parties.

But there’s another way of viewing this and that comes from the opposite angle. Maybe this is the perfect time, based on the qualifications needed to operate within the modern version of United.

There is no doubt that Pochettino has lost some of his sheen since his masterful handling of Daniel Levy at Tottenham, but what did he gain? He managed the vastest collection of footballing egos at PSG, worked under a convoluted tier of meddlers in the madhouse of Chelsea and was confronted by presidential interference in his time with the US national team at the World Cup.

Two schools of thought can exist here. One is that he failed to tear up any trees in each of those assignments. But the other talks to the point we are making: United require a manager who can navigate their unique brand of chaos and the new guy knows the dance. 

Pochettino won’t ever thank Donald Trump for the Folarin Balogun fiasco in the summer, but Sir Jim Ratcliffe would have to work awfully hard to cause him a more uncomfortable press conference.

The scale of Pochettino’s challenge is obvious. In the micro, that means applying a playing style built on hard running to a squad that jogged its way to embarrassing statistics under Carrick. In the macro, it will be his challenge with Wilcox and a recruitment team that effectively cost Carrick his job.

Talking to one of Pochettino’s former colleagues on Friday, the expectation is that greater control over transfers will have been a key tenet of those negotiations with United. 

As predictable as that might sound, it was a huge bone of contention for him at Chelsea and United’s failures in this area are clear. Time will tell if any promises are honoured.

But Pochettino has got what he wanted and pursued. His desire for the post has never been disguised, which can be mapped as a trail of breadcrumbs from that bottle of red he once shared with Sir Alex Ferguson all the way up to carefully planted mentions of the club in gatherings with media. 

There were some acts of reassurance necessary for the final step, of course, and doubtless it will sting to leave the US - his farewell tears on Friday showed as much. But not enough to inspire a second thought.

To look back over Pochettino’s other stints in England, one main memory stands out from his time at Tottenham and I’ve cited in this space previously. 

It traces to September 2016, when Pochettino was on the rise and had a game approaching against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City. In attempting to coax a decent line in the press conference, a few of us killed time before his arrival by digging up old footage of Pochettino’s Espanyol beating Barcelona, when he and Guardiola were on opposing sides.

Within the clip was an unexpected gem, because Pochettino murdered the Brazilian Ronaldo in a challenge. He took the ball, sure, but demolished the man, too, and his boot ended up shoulder-high. We were watching this when Pochettino wandered over and requested a replay – when it was shown, he laughed maniacally.

As a player, he always saw the value in a good reducer. And it’s a trait that might well be needed at United. If Wilcox and the other cronies upstairs don’t up their game, they might find that Carrington offers fewer hiding places than the old Wembley.

Was Tom Brady ever in the Blues' building? 

Tom Brady has left Birmingham, but was he ever really there? Across three years, he attended only four games.

The club is on a steep upward trajectory and there is no doubt that the Brady association helped on their commercial side. 

But I recall speaking to one Blues shareholder a couple of seasons back, and after attempting to establish some tangible detail about their star investor’s contribution, there was a period of silence. When I asked how often Brady might dial into meetings, there was laughter. 

In this era of celebrity ownership of our football clubs, it’s easy to get blinded by a famous name. And easier still to get drawn in by suggestions of expertise that they have carried over from a different space. 

But in the vast majority of cases, they are little more than mascots without the costume. 

Great delivery from Cummins - but it's not over yet

Pat Cummins stood for 70 minutes on Thursday and answered questions about Sandpapergate. 

The Australia captain refused to budge, both from the microphone and his position that Usman Khawaja was incorrect in his claim that the entire team was in on the plot to cheat against South Africa in 2018. 

It’s hard to know what was more impressive – Cummins’ commitment to answering every question, or his delusion in believing that it would be the last time he discusses it.
news.summary: United needed a big bull to replace Carrick and they have one. Wilcox's preference? Eddie Howe who is far from a shrinking violet, but he's not Pochettino. And Pochettino certainly isn't Carrick.
news.author: Editor,Riath Al-Samarrai

news.title: Trump to meet Quad leaders in Manila: White House
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 14 (IANS) US President Donald Trump will meet the leaders of the Quad countries in Manila during his upcoming visit to the Philippines, the White House said, placing the Indo-Pacific partnership on an itinerary that will also take him to China. The meeting will bring the United States together with India, Japan and Australia. The White House outlined broad regional priorities for the discussions but did not announce specific agreements expected from them. "In Manila, the President will participate in a multilateral meeting with Quad leaders to discuss shared interests of peace, prosperity, and security in the Indo-Pacific region," White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told reporters in a pre-trip briefing. Wales described the Quad as a "partnership of action", and said it was addressing regional challenges and creating opportunities for a free and open Indo-Pacific. The White House did not announce a separate meeting between Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the briefing. Nor did it provide a detailed Quad agenda beyond the regional priorities set out by Wales. Trump is scheduled to leave Washington early Monday (local time) and arrive in Manila on Tuesday evening, local time, Wales said. The Quad meeting is listed ahead of a planned trade agreement signing with Thailand, a US-ASEAN special summit and a dinner with regional leaders. On Wednesday, Trump is scheduled to attend a welcome ceremony at the Philippine presidential palace, followed by bilateral talks and a lunch banquet. Wales said the visit would include commercial deals and strategic investments involving American aviation, defence, energy and technology companies. The President will then travel to Shenzhen for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' dinner. Meetings with APEC leaders and a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled for Thursday, Wales said. Trump is also due to meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a discussion that will include nuclear weapons. A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the administration did not expect the three-way meeting to produce an agreement. The Quad brings together Australia, India, Japan and the United States for cooperation on issues including maritime security, critical minerals, energy and disaster response. The grouping's foreign ministers met in Atlanta on October 31. Their joint statement welcomed a US commitment of $10 million to support infrastructure and facilities recovering critical minerals from waste in India and ASEAN countries, among other initiatives.

news.title: Live updates: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop
news.text:
BREAKING: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication ” that anything “nefarious” was behind the ground stop, but blamed a telecommunications outage.

Transportation Secretary Duffy said tonight that switches in the air traffic control system became overloaded with data.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said at a briefing at the White House.

“We have TDM telecoms, so this is analog telecom,” Duffy said.”Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data.”

He said the routers “started to give us inconsistency in the data.”

Duffy said new switches worked, but it was the old hardware that went down. He called on Congress to fund improvements to the air traffic control system. He said President Donald Trump has requested the money from Congress for improvements.

The ground stop was sparked after “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country,” Secretary Duffy said.

TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center.

“We have procedures for this,” Duffy said at a news conference tonight.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy listens at a White House briefing tonight, lifting the ground stop. Alex Wong / Getty

“We didn’t lose all telecom, we didn’t lose all radar,” Duffy said. “But that instability, because of an abundance of caution and making sure we keep the American public safe, we did the ground stop.”

There were around 3,500 planes in the air when the ground stop was called at 3:36 p.m. Duffy said that last time he checked, there were around 400 in the airspace.

DHS Secretary Mullin says that there is no sign of a cyberattack in today’s ground stoppage.

“So far what we’ve seen there is no cyberattack. We’re still working through that process,” he said. “Our teams are working through that process.”

He said that things were progressing “in the right direction.”

Mullin said the public was never in any danger and the ground stop was out of an abundance of caution.

15m ago / 8:36 PM ESTThe national ground stop has been liftedThe FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop, more than five hours after the initial public alert.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the airspace opened at 8:15 this evening.

The national FAA ground stop will be lifted imminently, a source familiar with the matter tells NBC News.

Orlando International Airport on Friday. Finn Gomez / Getty

However, resolving the impact will likely take time given many airline crews and planes are out of place, and considering pilot and flight attendant max duty time.

Shivani Hawkins had just landed in Los Angeles from the Bay Area when she learned about the nationwide ground stop.

She was traveling with her two young children and arrived for a flight tonight to Australia.

“We don’t have any idea what’s happening with our flight for the next six hours,” she said.

Shivani said the airline gave her family $30 food vouchers each, unprompted. “We’re just hanging out in the LAX area because Friday rush hour traffic has been brutal.”

Most days this week saw about 100 flight cancelations into and out of the U.S. — so far today, upwards of 5,300 flights have been canceled.

The Association of Organ Procurement Organizations, a national nonprofit that represents the U.S. organ donation community, said it is closely monitoring the ground stop.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Friday. Kamil Krzaczynski / AFP via Getty

The group said when a flight is disrupted, organ procurement organizations (OPO) work to find safe alternatives, including ground transportation.

The association said in a statement it works “around the clock” to “give every donated organ the best possible chance to save a life.”

“Hearts and lungs are among the most time-sensitive organs to transport. If a delay threatens an organ’s viability, the OPO shares the updated arrival estimate with the receiving transplant team, which uses its clinical judgment to determine whether the transplant can safely proceed,” Allison Erickson, the AOPO president, said.

“We hope the ground stop is resolved soon for everyone affected.”

Gillian Horn and her fiance were on a Delta flight at John F. Kennedy International Airport, bound for a long-planned family trip to Morocco, when the pilot announced the national ground stop over the speakers this afternoon.

“It was obviously met by a huge chorus of groans. Everyone was kind of like, ‘No way!’” she told NBC News.

The couple already had a nightmare two days of travel as their original flight yesterday was cancelled due to weather.

Today, they arrived at the airport around 2 p.m. for their 4 p.m. flight to Atlanta then on to Marrakesh, when the ground stop was announced and they had to deplane.

The couple scrambled to rebook flights and decided to book one out of the U.S. in hopes of avoiding the ground stop to make it to Morocco. In total, they’ve been rebooked six times since yesterday.

She described Terminal Four as packed, the Delta help desk line “astronomically long,” and many passengers leaving altogether.

Horn said around 6 p.m. she observed that flights to Europe were still planning to depart.

“We were sitting at a random gate, and it was at Catania, Italy. Out of the blue around 6 p.m. they go whoever to Catania, this flight is going to board in an hour,” she said. “There were claps, actual cheering and claps from the section.”

That inspired her and her fiancé to wait it out. Their flight to Paris was originally set to depart at 7 p.m. but got delayed twice to 9 p.m. She’s hopeful to board soon.

“It could be worse,” she said. “If we were stuck on the tarmac. Could be worse if we weren’t together. … At the end of the day, it’s fine. We want to get there safely. But we want to get there.”

The last time the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, after files in a system critical for pilots were accidentally deleted.

The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

The system that was damaged was NOTAM, or Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to potential dangers.

There was no evidence of a cyberattack, the Federal Aviation Administration said at the time. Instead, the department blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases.

The FAA said it made the necessary repairs to the system and had taken steps to make it more resilient.

President Donald Trump is getting constant updates on the situation with the nationwide ground stop, according to a senior White House official.

The FAA ordered the ground stop this afternoon, and it will run through at least 11 tonight.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”

There have been more than 10,00 U.S. flights delayed and over 4,000 cancellations today amid an extremely rare nationwide ground stop, according to a tracking website.

Denver International Airport on Friday. J. David Ake / Getty

At 7:30 tonight, FlightAware showed 10,079 US-related delays and 4,238 US-related cancelations.

Those numbers are far higher than in previous days. Yesterday, there were around 6,800 U.S.-related delays and 1,024 U.S.-related cancellations, according to the site.

Wednesday only had 3,424 delays and 99 cancellations in the U.S., it said.

Travelers have formed a long line at Chicago O’Hare International Airport’s baggage services desk. Among their questions: Where is their luggage? When will they get it?

2h ago / 7:18 PM ESTSpaceX allowed to launch rocket despite ground stop SpaceX was able to launch a rocket during the ground stop because the agency already had flight prohibitions around the launch site before the national ground stop was initiated.

“The FAA had already cleared airplanes around it, so it gave a nice path all the way up into space,” Jeff Guzzetti, an aviation safety expert, said. “All of that airspace above Texas and through the trajectory of the rocket was already cleared. There were already flight prohibitions in place.”

Guzzetti previously worked for the FAA and was involved in rocket launch preparations for the agency.

SpaceX launched its 15th uncrewed flight of its Starship rocket with the hopes that it would be the first round-trip rocket voyage back to the spot where it left Earth.

The launch took place in Texas just a few minutes after its opening window and the Starship entered orbit around the Earth just after 5 p.m. local time.

However, the company abandoned plans to return the rocket’s booster and collect it at the launch pad. Instead, the booster splashed down into the Gulf of Mexico after the company aborted the maneuver. SpaceX hopes to retrieve the upper stage of the rocket tomorrow after it orbits Earth about 14 times and returns to Earth.

An outage that affected millions of Microsoft customers around the world does not appear to be linked to the ground stop, the company said.

“Microsoft has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the recent service disruption,” a spokesperson said.

Danielle Curry heard about the nationwide ground stop on her way to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport but still went to inquire about her flight.

“They don’t know if the flights are going to even go today, so they let me change it to tomorrow,” she said.

“I just wanted to get home,” she said. “But my aunt lives here, so I’m going back to my aunt’s house, so I’m lucky compared to most.”

But the uncertainty about the cause of the extraordinary ground stoppage, coupled with world events, left Curry uneasy.

“It’s a little scary, like, is it cyberattack? Like, what is actually happening?” she said.

Officials have said that there were no initial indications of a cyberattack, but that a cause for the telecommunication outage had not yet been determined.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations, and NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time for them to travel to their games this weekend.

Most college football teams playing tomorrow travel the day before their game, and the stoppage left many schools — including No. 2 Utah, eighth-ranked Texas and No. 9 Tennessee — at a standstill as they departed for road games.

Meanwhile, the Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly today for games on Saturday. They had just boarded the team plane in New Orleans after playing the Pelicans earlier this week when their flight to Memphis was halted in place.

There are 14 scheduled games in the NHL tomorrow. And while the Panthers made it to St. Louis for their game before the stoppage began, the Sharks were among those that were left waiting to leave for their game in Utah.

The FAA did not provide a timeline for restarting flights, leaving sporting events taking place beyond tomorrow in limbo. That includes most of the Week 10 schedule in the NFL along with numerous college sporting events.

The National Weather Service said its radars are fully operational and working normally.

“Outdated content from isolated webpages stating otherwise has been circulating, but NWS radars are operating normally,” the agency said.

NBC News’ weather unit confirmed that a page on the agency’s site associated with public-facing radar data was down, but the site is now operational and all radar sites across sites across the U.S. were working.

FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, is among the parcel delivery services that are monitoring the ground stop, saying customers can track the status of their shipments through the company’s website.

“We are prepared to activate contingency plans to minimize service disruptions and will resume normal flight operations as soon as the FAA permits,” said Shannon Davis, a spokesperson for FedEx.

The FAA’s ground stop applies to all departing flights at U.S. airports and therefore affects cargo and package shipping operations that rely on air transport.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

FedEx has nearly 700 aircraft that operate around the globe, shipping an average of 17 million packages and 20 million pounds of freight daily, according to the company’s website. Most of those shipments are made in the U.S.

Gerardo Lopez was hoping to escape Chicago for sunny San Diego but was one of the travelers whose plans have been put on ice by the nationwide ground stoppage.

“It’s my only trip this year, so yes, it’s frustrating,” he told NBC Chicago at Chicago Midway International Airport. “I don’t get too much vacation.”

“I just wish they’d get their act together soon, so we can get out of here,” he said. “If not, I’ve got to head back home.”

We are more than three hours into the nationwide ground stop, which is an extremely rare occurrence.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Even though it’s a rail service, Amtrak said air travel issues are creating frustrations for its passengers.

“We’re currently experiencing higher-than-normal call volumes due to ongoing airline issues,” it said on social media.

Sierra Gould was on the last leg of a flight from Denver to her home in Corpus Christi, Texas, when the connecting flight from Houston was stuck on the ground by the national flight stoppage.

“Trying to remain calm, because panicking isn’t going to do any thing,” she said at Houston International Airport.

She hoped her flight would still happen, but wasn’t optimistic.

“I think I’m going to have someone drive out here and pick me up and go home,” Gould said. “Thank God I’m only three hours away.”

But a big concern is her luggage, because it was to be part of the connecting flight.

There’s a general sense of confusion among passengers at Denver International Airport amid a lack of information.

Very few travelers seem to grasp the big picture — that all outgoing planes across the nation have been grounded — and many airport TVs are broadcasting sports.

People in lines to rebook flights are seemingly unaware of the scale of the travel headache that’s unfolding across the U.S. There are big crowds and long lines for everything because people are stuck at the airport and aren’t leaving as usual.

Many people are calling their families and customer service to seek info and updates. The lines for food are growing longer and seating is getting harder to come by.

San Francisco International Airport said minutes ago that Pacific-bound flights have been cleared to leave, including to Hawaii and Asia.

It said that the clearance occurred at 3 p.m. local time (6 p.m. ET).

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.

“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, said its software didn’t cause today’s nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

The startup, which is based in Boston, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

3h ago / 6:09 PM ESTRedundancies in place so pilots can still receive information to safely land, aviation expert saysThere are multiple layers of communications for air traffic, and aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said that it’s the high-altitude control centers that are experiencing the outage today.

Pilots are trained to handle radio outages such as this and there are other means to relay information to them to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing, he said.

“There are redundancies in place so pilots can get this information and a lot of times the information can be communicated digitally on a screen in the cockpit,” he said.

“When you’re flying in high altitude in a cruise flight, you’re talking to an air route traffic control center that’s run by the FAA and that’s the one that’s having the problem,” Guzzetti said.

“Then they will hand you off to an approach controller that’s near a major city. You talk to the approach controller, which is a mid-level altitude, as you are making your descent to the airport, and then that controller hands you off one last time to the local controller, who’s at the control tower.”

At this early stage of the investigation into today’s communications outage, there is no indication that the incident was caused by malicious activity, multiple officials from multiple agencies involved tell NBC News.

They say they haven’t seen any evidence of the type of activity normally associated with a cyberattack.

A passenger sits next to the departure board at Miami International Airport. Joe Raedle / Getty

But the officials cautioned that it is early in the investigation and that the findings change as they continue to dig into the problem.

Three senior officials said there’s nothing that indicates a connection between today’s FAA incident and Microsoft’s widespread outage.

Today’s nationwide ground stop comes soon after the FAA implemented changes to the air traffic control system that it said would add the use of AI. It’s not clear, though, if the two are related.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy unveiled the system — known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART — in September, saying it “centralizes 200 data streams” into one platform. The benefits would include fewer delays and cancellations, he said.

The SMART platform drew skepticism from the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which said in a statement in September that it was not involved in the design, testing or implementation of the system. Democratic lawmakers also pushed back, asking the FAA in a letter Oct. 9 to pause the changes.

But after testing the system at airports in the Washington area, the FAA said this week that the platform was active nationwide and would use AI to help inform routing and schedule recommendations, according to reports in Flying magazine and Ars Technica.

“Using AI, SMART analyzes airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur,” the FAA says in a description of the program.

Planes are parked at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. John Locher / AP

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked by a reporter outside the White House about a possible connection between AI and the ground stop. He responded: “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We’re going through that process, and we’re going to find out what happened.”

A Republican leadership aide told NBC News early this evening that senior members have not yet received a briefing from administration officials on the nationwide ground stop.

Separately, a senior lawmaker told NBC News that they have gotten no information. When they inquired with officials, the lawmaker says they were told there is no information to share at this point.

The FAA blamed today’s ground stop on a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage — out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” it said on X.

“Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” it said.

Delta Airlines planes are seen at LaGuardia Airport in New York, today. Ryan Murphy / AP

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said that today’s outage is “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti, who said he doesn’t know the cause of the outage, stressed that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

He added that the situation is moving from a safety issue to a massive logistics problem.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is still communication with planes despite the ground stop.

“My understanding is that we can still communicate,” Mullin said this afternoon. “It’s just that it’s at different levels and clarity that we can get to.”

“But there’s redundancy in most communications,” he said. “So, as you can see, there’s still planes landing, and so there’s still communications going on.”

With all departing flights grounded, some airports are beginning to run out of space for jets.

A source with knowledge of the situation told NBC News that Reagan National Airport is at capacity and that Chicago O’Hare is nearing capacity, meaning there is no place for planes to park and that some of the planes may have to divert to other airports.

4h ago / 5:31 PM ESTSec. Mullin says FAA ground stop was caused by 'telecommunication outage'01:51Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters the nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration was the result of a telecommunication outage. He also assured that the issue was not the result of some form of attack or hack.

Deveren Werne was in Indianapolis headed to Chicago this afternoon on an American Airlines flight when the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now our plane is heading back to the terminal so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin at the White House. Alex Brandon / AP

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication as of yet” that there was anything “nefarious” that caused the ground stop. He said it was the result of a telecommunications outage “as of now.”

Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed and they “are not ruling out anything at this point” in terms of what caused the communications issue. He said those currently on flights have no reason for concern.

“We are assured that everybody is safe,” he said, adding that it was unprecedented.

A flight board showing delayed flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, today in Arlington, Va. Tom Brenner / AP

Planes across the country were grounded and not allowed to take off this afternoon after a “ground stop” was issued.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the ground stop at 4:16 p.m. today on X.

He said the Federal Aviation Administration “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

The order means flights are prevented from taking off.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” Duffy said. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”
news.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication ” that anything “nefarious” was behind the ground stop, but blamed a telecommunications outage.Instability with radar data prompted ground stop, Duffy saysNo sign of cyberattack, DHS secretary saysThe national ground stop has been lifted
