They started to give us inconsistency in the data ... and because of that, we shut the system down," Duffy said.According to an airline source cited by CNN, the network router problem spread across the country, affecting communications at multiple air traffic control facilities. The FAA said the ground stop was imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety".The telecommunications failure affected all 22 regional air route traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft across the US.The disruption raised concerns over air traffic controllers' ability to communicate reliably with pilots, prompting the FAA to suspend departures as a precautionary measure.Was FAA outage caused by a cyberattack?US officials said there was no indication so far that the communications failure was the result of a deliberate attack.US President Donald Trump said the disruption was unlikely to have been caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence. Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin also said preliminary assessments did not point to a national security threat."This isn’t the same comparison to 9/11," Mullin told reporters outside the White House, adding that all flights had been accounted for and passengers were safe."There is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States," he said.Preliminary reports also indicated that the incident was not a cyberattack, law enforcement sources told CNN. Air Canada said flights between Canada, the Caribbean and South America that transit US airspace could also be affected by the disruption.What happens next?Transportation secretary Sean Duffy warned that further disruptions to air travel were likely unless the country's ageing air traffic control systems were modernised. He urged Congress to approve legislation providing additional funding to upgrade the infrastructure."You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that," Duffy said.The FAA and other federal authorities continued working to identify the cause of the telecommunications failure and restore normal operations.However, with no definite timeline for resolution, airlines were preparing for an extended disruption. Passengers were advised to check with their carriers for updates before heading to airports.Trump had been briefed on the situation, while Mullin said the administration was coordinating the response to ensure officials had the necessary resources.The immediate priority remained restoring communications across the affected air traffic control centres and allowing flight departures to resume safely.You use AI every day. news.title: Trump Offers Bizarre Explanation for Nationwide Flight Chaos
news.text:
Donald Trump offered a curious explanation for the nationwide aviation meltdown that brought air travel to a standstill on Friday.

The president, 80, blamed the nationwide ground stop, which lasted more than four hours, on a “bunch of old broken stuff” in the air traffic control infrastructure.

Trump reportedly gave that vague explanation for the disruption to Fox News reporter Peter Doocy, who spoke with him by phone.

“He says it does not seem like this is a cyberattack or AI or anything like that,” Doocy told Laura Ingraham. “I asked him a couple different ways, and he said it doesn’t seem like that, and that that is the first thing that they always look for.”

“He said there’s nobody taking credit which would be common if somebody did execute a huge cyber attack like this on critical infrastructure but that he would let us know and the team would let us know if that is something that happened,” he continued. 

Trump had remained effectively silent on the unfolding chaos, which began at around 4 p.m. EST Friday, when the FAA grounded all flights nationwide until 11 p.m. Some flights began resuming shortly after 8 p.m.

“He said instead this seems to be a situation where there’s a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA relies on to keep planes in the sky. He said there’s a bunch of—some of this is like 55-year-old equipment that needs to keep working, keep running, and that they have worked on it, they’ve talked to Congress about replacing, it just hasn’t gotten replaced yet. So that is the first information that we have from the president.”

This is a developing story that will be updated.

The president, 80, blamed the nationwide ground stop, which lasted more than four hours, on a “bunch of old broken stuff” in the air traffic control infrastructure.

news.title: US FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop At All Airports After Telecom Outage; 7,000 Flights Hit
news.text:
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop across all American airports following a telecommunications outage that disrupted air traffic control operations across the country. The disruption affected thousands of flights, with approximately 7,000 services either delayed or cancelled, according to flight-tracking platform FlightAware.
US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy confirmed the development in a post on X, saying a communication failure had affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians were investigating the issue, he added.
"The FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," Duffy stated.
The FAA said the disruption was caused by a temporary telecommunications outage and that flights had been halted as a precaution.
"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the agency said on X.
US Flight Disruption: 7,000 Services Delayed Or Cancelled
The communication failure reportedly affected all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers in the United States, which guide aircraft within their respective regions, particularly those approaching airports.
According to FlightAware, around 7,000 flights were either delayed or cancelled following the FAA's ground stop order.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported that approximately 4,042 flights were airborne and heading towards US airports when the order was issued.
The FAA said every flight had been accounted for, while international services would be handled on a case-by-case basis.

'This Is Not Another 9/11': US Homeland Security Secretary
US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the nationwide aviation disruption had been triggered by a threat to the country.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Mullin assured the public that all flights had been accounted for and passengers were safe. However, he cautioned that restoring normal operations could take time.
"Everybody’s safe. The flights are accounted for," he said, adding, "This is not another 9/11."
He further stated, "It's going to take some time."
Mullin said authorities had not ruled out any possible explanation for the telecommunications outage, including a potential connection with the planned rollout of a new artificial intelligence tool designed to assist air traffic controllers.

When asked whether the AI tool could have contributed to the disruption, he said, "You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We are going through that process."
The Homeland Security Secretary also sought to reassure people with family members travelling by air.
"Everybody is safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying."
He reiterated that the ground stop was a precautionary measure following the telecommunications failure and that there was no indication of a deliberate attack so far.
"This was a telecommunications outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the fights. There is no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack," Mullin said.
US President Donald Trump was also briefed on the situation, the Homeland Security Secretary confirmed.
The nationwide ground stop marks the second such instance since the September 11, 2001 attacks, according to the information provided, underlining the scale of the disruption to aviation operations across the country.

news.title: It's now clear that tech bros are too powerful
news.text:
As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.” 

Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move.

Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At the US midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood?

This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind.

Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: No one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. 

Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders — they can blitz an entire veg patch.

That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer. It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom. Smart!

Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world, including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whiskey with him. Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives: “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”.

Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. 

That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing.

Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action.

Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “dilapidated storefront” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. 

Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws.

In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board moved with incredible sloth. 

It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” — before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. 

Huang eventually resigned from Nvidia on Thursday and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress. But the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates. 

You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia. One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. 

A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes.

This scandal is different from the allegations over David Walliams or the convictions handed down against Russell Brand — but one black thread that connects them is the grace afforded to each man by enablers and the powerful. 

Asked about the Huang affair, Trump described him as a “fine person”. Many of us will remember Trump defending the white nationalists who stormed Charlottesville in 2017. They were “some very fine people”, he said.
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts
news.author: Aditya Chakrabortt,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Rubio takes swipe at international law, attacks ICC
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim Friday at what he deemed the 'weaponization of international law,' calling it a tool of the elite, and issued a stark warning to the International Criminal Court.Rubio cautioned the ICC against 'quoting laws to men with swords,' as he accused the Hague-based tribunal of trying to enforce rules that Washington does not recognize.His remarks to the Federalist Society National Lawyers Convention came around a month after the United States announced new sanctions on the ICC, vowing to cripple its operations.The court prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.The US signed the Rome Statute establishing the ICC but never ratified the treaty. Israel, Russia and China are also not ICC members.Rubio's keynote address at the conservative group, where he received a standing ovation, marks his first major US speech since the Republican Party's sweeping losses in midterm elections earlier this month.Rubio said Friday that international law had been invoked against 'nearly every major foreign policy decision' of the Trump administration, from boat strikes in the Caribbean to the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.He charged that such law was not neutral, but has been an 'instrument' for the global elite to advance their interests.The top US diplomat previously said Washington would bar transactions with what he called a 'rogue court,' stepping up a long-running campaign by US President Donald Trump's government against the ICC.Washington has vowed to dismantle the court, angered as judges issued an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged crimes in Gaza.Rubio on Friday renewed criticism of the ICC, calling it accountable to no one although 'armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute and to jail our citizens, according to laws we neither consent nor control.'He added: 'If they're foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city's charters against his legions.''He said: 'Stop quoting laws to men with swords.''The venue of Rubio's remarks, a gathering of the legal profession, could further speculation that he is looking beyond his foreign policy portfolio. Past presidential hopefuls have also addressed the conference.Rubio is widely seen as a possible successor to Trump, although he has dismissed reports that he was planning to leave the administration to prepare for a 2028 election run.
news.author: Agence France-Presse

news.title: How China mastered the art of the honeytrap: As Nvidia boss Jensen Huang sees an affair detonate his career, we reveal how Beijing is finding new ways to exploit the libidos of powerful men in the West
news.text:
The Jensen Huang scandal shows that no matter how sophisticated artificial intelligence becomes, there’s no accounting for human stupidity.

The now ex-boss of Nvidia, who has admitted to an affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang – and is also accused of having relationships with two employees – once boasted that cyber security was the next big market for artificial intelligence (AI).

But who needs tenacious hackers when the boss of the world’s most cutting-edge firm can seemingly fall victim to one of the oldest espionage tools – one described by Chairman Mao as the ‘beautiful woman stratagem’, or meiren ji in Mandarin?

It was not the first time, and it will not be the last time, that a powerful man with a global-sized ego has apparently walked into a honeytrap. They have long been popular with Chinese intelligence agencies – as a means of both espionage and entrapment, at home and abroad.

But as the tech race with the US heats up, so Silicon Valley and its hapless tech nerds have become a prime target.

China’s spy chief, Chen Yixin, recently described AI as ‘the main battleground in global technological competition’ and companies appear to be aware of the threat, running clunky training courses on how to spot a dodgy approach.

OpenAI, whose AI models are among the world’s most sophisticated, reportedly puts its mostly male techies through a range of scenarios, including the late-night knock on the hotel room door.

First there’s a blonde with champagne, then, when that doesn’t work, the spies send a redhead – and next a young man. Only the staff who resist these temptations reportedly survive.

But when Huang, the most powerful man in tech, apparently falls into a honeytrap, it suggests the training sessions still have a long way to go.

Here in the UK, MI5 has warned that Chinese intelligence services are trying to cultivate ‘long-term relationships’ and have been known to ‘exploit vulnerabilities such as sexual relationships... to pressurise individuals to co-operate with them’.

In evidence to Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee, MI6 described the ‘gamut of blackmail, honeytrapping’ employed by China.

Silicon Valley brings to mind the hapless Roddy Ho from the Apple TV series Slow Horses.

The arrogant, socially inept computer nerd, played by Christopher Chung – who struggles to communicate with anything without a screen – is easy pickings for ‘Tara’, the ‘girlfriend’ who turns out to be a terrorist plotting a cyber attack.

For the Roddys of the tech world, seduction most often happens via their screen. Both UK and US intelligence agencies have warned about fake LinkedIn profiles, usually featuring photos of alluring Asian women, real or AI-generated, and designed to build online relationships with targets.

The aim is to persuade them to share information or to entice them to dubious overseas ‘conferences’ where a formal approach can be made or the techie can be sexually compromised.

Last month, Changli ‘Sophia’ Luo, a glamorous China-born entrepreneur, pleaded guilty in a court in Manhattan to wire fraud after attempting to extort more than $1billion (£753million) from Wesley Edens, a financier and the co-owner of Aston Villa.

They’d met on LinkedIn and she threatened to release a secret recording of their sexual encounter later unless he paid up. No evidence was presented to the court of hostile intelligence links, though every Chinese citizen is obliged by law to assist the country’s spy agencies on demand.

MI5 recently warned about Chinese spies posing as ‘headhunters’, naming Amanda Qiu, chief executive of BP-YR Executive Search, a company in Beijing, and Shirly Shen of Internship Union, based in Hong Kong, as fronts for the Ministry of State Security (MSS), China’s main spy agency.

The fake profiles were used to target people with valuable knowledge or skills. ‘The headhunters are typically China-based individuals who make initial contact with a target before referring them to an officer,’ the MI5 alert said.

‘It is a phenomenon. And I will tell you, it is weird,’ says James Mulvenon, chief intelligence officer of Pamir Consulting, which provides risk assessments for companies investing in China.

‘I’m getting an enormous number of very sophisticated LinkedIn requests from the same type of attractive young Chinese woman,’ he told The Times.

He described how two such women showed up at an ‘investment risks’ conference he hosted in Virginia in the US, attempting to gain entry. ‘We didn’t let them in, but they had all the information [about the event] and everything else.’

Recently declassified documents show how suspected spy Christine Fang targeted a swathe of Democratic Party politicians across the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond before fleeing back to China in 2015.

This included former congressman Eric Swalwell, who sat on an influential intelligence committee. It has even been reported that sex workers in some of the most prosperous Bay regions, including Menlo Park (home of Facebook, now Meta) have been paid by foreign spies for information about their clients.

Then there is Katrina Leung, a Los Angeles-based consultant and Republican fundraiser suspected to be a Chinese spy who had affairs with two FBI agents who were overseeing her case.

She convinced them she was working for the Bureau, too, while continuing to pass secrets to Beijing before her arrest in 2003.

While technology is a focus of Chinese espionage, ‘beautiful woman stratagem’, or meiren ji, is not confined to the world of the nerds. ‘We are constantly having to remove people from our embassies and consulates in China because they get into these honeytraps,’ Dennis Wilder, a former CIA China analyst and now senior fellow at Georgetown University, told the Washington Post.

In 2013, when British pharmaceutical giant GSK was embroiled in a corruption scandal in China, a secretly filmed video of its China head, Mark Reilly, having sex with his Chinese girlfriend in his Shanghai apartment was emailed to the company’s chief executive and other board members.

The purpose of this meiren ji appeared to be to put pressure on GSK during the corruption investigation. Gaining entry to the apartment and placing the device would have been tricky, and was assumed to have been the work of skilled intelligence operatives.

The Chinese security services have used compromising video material in several other politically convenient corruption cases.

Around the same time as Mark Reilly’s case, China punished 15 government officials in Chongqing after they too appeared in secretly recorded sex videos.

Foremost among them was Lei Zhengfu, a powerful local Communist Party secretary, who was jailed for 13 years. Officially, it was described as a case of ‘criminal extortion’ by a ‘local businessman’. But Xi Jinping, newly installed as China’s all-powerful leader, had been in a fierce power struggle with the local party boss Bo Xilai, an ally of Lei.

During my time as a correspondent in Beijing, there was a notorious bar in the diplomatic quarter called Maggies – packed with sex workers and owned by former security officials – known as ‘honey-pot central’ and widely believed to be under the control of the Public Security Bureau.

It remained a favourite hangout of Beijing’s less cautious expatriate community, and I still wonder how many dusty and lurid tapes are filed away, waiting for use.

Shenzhen in southern China, just across the border from Hong Kong, is the country’s technology capital, but for a long time it was also known as ‘mistress village’. It was where businessmen based in the former British colony kept their ‘minor wives’, with whom they spent time when ostensibly visiting their Chinese factories. It also left them wide open to extortion and entrapment.

Hong Kong is also where Rupert Murdoch met his third wife Wendi Deng, who at the time had been working as an intern at Star TV, which was owned by Murdoch’s News Corp.

She secured the internship, it has been widely reported, when, as a student, she bought a first-class ticket from New York to Hong Kong, and ‘coincidentally’ found herself sitting next to Bruce Churchill, then chief operating officer of Star TV. He fixed her up with a job.

There have been constant rumours that Deng, who is also alleged to have been romantically linked to Tony Blair and Eric Schmidt, then CEO of Google, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

In his biography of the media mogul, Michael Wolff wrote that Murdoch, after his divorce from Deng, claimed repeatedly that she had been a Chinese spy throughout their marriage. In 2017, it was reported that US counterintelligence officials warned Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s billionaire son-in-law, that Deng could be using her close friendship with Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump – the president’s daughter – to further the interests of the Chinese government.

But it is undoubtedly in China that honeytraps have their richest history – though not without some bizarre twists.

In May 1986, Bernard Boursicot, a French diplomat, went on trial in Paris for spying for Beijing, having been recruited by his Chinese lover, Shi Peipu, a singer at the Beijing Opera. The strangest thing about the case was that Shi turned out to be a man – and Boursicot claimed not to have noticed during their 18-year relationship, due to Shi’s unique ability to retract his testicles.

Of course, China is not the only country to employ honeytraps. In 1986, Israel kidnapped Mordechai Vanunu, who had revealed the existence of his country’s nuclear programme, by luring him from his hideout in London to Rome using a sultry Mossad agent Cheryl Bentov, codenamed ‘Cindy’, who had struck up a relationship with the balding engineer.

In an inversion of the traditional honeytrap, during the Cold War the East German secret police, the Stasi, even set up a special department staffed with what they called ‘Romeo spies’. Their task was to infiltrate the West in search of powerful women, strike up a romance and tap them for secrets.

Gathering kompromat (compromising material) was also a routine tool of the Soviet KGB, and remains so for Russia. There have been rumours, furthered by the emergence of the Steele Dossier in 2017, a 35-page collection of intelligence memos compiled by former MI6 officer Christopher Steele – though no evidence – that the Russians hold compromising material on Donald Trump, related to hotly denied and unprintable alleged exploits with sex workers during trips in Moscow before he became president.

But the role of honeytraps in China’s intelligence operations has its roots in necessity as much as strategy. Beijing’s intelligence agencies were decimated by the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s, ten years of Maoist chaos, purges and fanaticism. The CIA estimated up to half the staff of Chinese embassies were brought home and human intelligence networks fell apart.

When Deng Xiaoping took over in 1978, two years after Mao’s death, he had to rebuild an intelligence network. He set up the MSS in 1983, relying on cyber spying and informal techniques (including meiren ji).

This ‘all of society’ approach, whereby everyone is regarded as a potential asset and every citizen is obliged by law to co-operate with the intelligence agencies, has become a hallmark of Chinese intelligence. As China began to open up to the West under Deng Xiaoping in the 1980s, so did the opportunities for entrapment, as gullible diplomats, politicians, businesspeople and academics at home and abroad sought a slice of China’s ‘economic miracle’.

Money, flattery and business or academic opportunities might all be floated – before the deployment of meiren ji. It seems a more sophisticated approach than many had assumed, frequently playing to the Western male fantasy about the ‘exotic’ Asian female.

The MSS often hires women from outside the formal organisation, with intelligence officers stepping in once a relationship has been established. This appears to have been the case with Jensen Huang, where the affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a tenacious businesswoman, seemed to come first, followed by recruitment.

The irony of the Nvidia case is that Jensen Huang hardly needed persuading to put his commercial interests above national interests, lobbying Trump hard to be allowed to sell his top-end AI chips to China despite Washington’s security concerns. There will almost certainly now be a backlash in Congress, pushing for tighter controls on the chips and the rolling up of a network of often dubious buyers across South-East Asia suspected of smuggling the devices to Beijing.

It is hard to say for sure what drives powerful men into a honeytrap. Ego, stupidity vulnerability and, of course, a desire for sex all play a part. It is shocking that an apparently brilliant computer scientist like Jensen Huang, one of the most important tech executives on the planet, apparently proved such an easy target.

Ian Williams is author of Vampire State: The Rise And Fall Of The Chinese Economy.
news.summary: Who needs tenacious hackers when the boss of the world's most cutting-edge firm can seemingly fall victim to one of the oldest espionage tools?
news.author: Editor,Ian Williams

news.title: Elon Musk backs petition seeking Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia
news.text: Washington DC Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Friday (local time) backed a purported petition seeking the reinstatement of Jensen Huang at Nvidia, expressing support for the former CEO days after his resignation amid controversy surrounding his alleged extramarital relationships. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too,” Musk said in a reply to a user on X on Friday. Musk backs Huang after resignation This comes after Huang resigned amid mounting scrutiny over reports of his alleged extramarital relationships, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by some US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence services. The controversy has drawn support for Huang from prominent figures, including US President Donald Trump and Musk, who has previously highlighted the importance of company founders and their contributions. Read: US Commerce Secretary Lutnick agrees to testify before Senate panel over Nvidia chip export controls Musk, earlier, had also expressed willingness to work with Huang after a user suggested that he hire the Nvidia co-founder. Responding to the post, Musk said, “That would be an honor.” Reports of relationships with two Nvidia employees The developments surrounding Huang have also taken a fresh turn following a report by Reuters that the former Nvidia CEO allegedly had an intimate relationship with a second company employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Earlier, The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports to him. The newspaper, citing five people who worked at the company, reported that the two were captured on video behaving affectionately at a hotel in San Jose, California, during an Nvidia conference in March. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and oversees programmes focused on applying the company’s chip technology to higher education and healthcare, particularly medical imaging devices, according to the company’s website. Alice Huang links add national security dimension The controversy initially intensified following reports of Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based data company Megaspeed International, one of Nvidia’s major customers. US intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence services, adding a national security dimension to the controversy. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang was the woman referred to in a letter Jensen Huang sent to Nvidia employees, in which he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised for violating her trust. The latest revelations have added to questions surrounding the former CEO’s personal conduct and leadership at the technology company. Huang’s legacy at Nvidia Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led its transformation into one of the world’s leading suppliers of artificial intelligence chips, becoming one of the most prominent figures in the global AI industry. Musk’s public endorsement of the purported reinstatement petition has now added another dimension to the controversy surrounding Huang’s departure from the company. Read: US Commerce Secretary Lutnick agrees to testify before Senate panel over Nvidia chip export controls https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/world/us-commerce-secretary-lutnick-agrees-to-testify-before-senate-panel-over-nvidia-chip-export-controls/article71700689.ece
news.summary: The public show of support comes as reports about the former chief executive’s personal relationships continue to draw attention

news.title: Bessent Blames Lutnick for Not Blacklisting Nvidia Partner Megaspeed
news.text: WASHINGTON: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that ‌four government agencies favored putting Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, on a trade black list but not the Commerce Department that was in charge.Bessent said Treasury, Pentagon, the State Department and the U.S. Trade Representative's Office had favored adding Megaspeed to the Commerce Department ​entity list for months. "But Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "You will have to ask them about their ​internal processes."The Commerce Department's so-called entity list is a trade blacklist of groups connected to China ⁠that US officials say pose national security risks. The department did not immediately return a request for comment.There is growing ​criticism of Lutnick's role in overseeing export controls on US chips to China. Lutnick reportedly stalled President Donald Trump's crackdown on ​companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's chips to China, media outlets reported this week.Republican Senator John Curtis said Friday that "Secretary Lutnick’s reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people."Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal ​said Friday "Lutnick must go. His malign self-enriching malfeasance shows the costs of corruption -- putting personal profit above public interest. Making ​powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security & economic competitiveness."Megaspeed has been in the spotlight following reports that Jensen ‌Huang ⁠had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy.Reuters reported Thursday that senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia's now-former CEO Jensen Huang.Bessent added that the administration was working to shut down "leakage" in the chip export system, and pointed to questions over how ​well Nvidia vetted its partner company ​amid CEO Jensen Huang's exit ⁠this week, which sent shockwaves across the AI industry.US lawmakers have called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips in the wake of the scandal, which has threatened ​to implicate some Trump administration members, including Lutnick, amid growing questions over the administration's oversight of chip sales ​to China."The real ⁠story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" Bessent said."It's important that anyone at ⁠the company ​there be held accountable for that."Asked if Congress needed to step in to ​act on export controls, he said: "We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented."Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott on Thursday ​asked Lutnick to testify.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Nvidia Approaches UK Chipmaker Arm CEO Rene Haas To Succeed Jensen Huang
news.text: Nvidia's board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times said on Friday, even as another report said some employees were pushing to bring back the former CEO.Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.Haas' name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang's exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013.He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia's finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO.Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature," the board said in a statement.Prior to Huang's resignation, a longtime Nvidia engineer had urged the board in an internal post to consider employee sentiment before taking any action, Wired reported late on Thursday.The post has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, with several urging the board to find a way to bring Huang back, the technology news platform said, citing internal correspondence it reviewed. Nvidia has about 42,000 employees worldwide.Billionaire Elon Musk separately said on X that a petition was underway to reinstate Huang and that he would sign it. It was not immediately clear whether Musk was referring to the internal effort reported by Wired.Nvidia declined to comment on the Wired report as well as Musk's post, while Arm also declined to comment. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.Haas became Arm CEO in 2022, overseeing the company's Nasdaq listing in 2023. Arm designs processor architectures and licenses them to other companies that develop chip designs. Historically its strength has been in mobile phones and it is expanding into computers.Haas' combination of familiarity with Nvidia and experience running a publicly traded chip company could make him an unusual fit for the role, said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities."Rene is one of few external candidates who wouldn't need to be brought up to speed on Nvidia," Boloor said, adding that Haas' understanding of the company's culture alongside his experience running Arm was "a combination you don't find very often."Arm's US-listed shares closed down about 5%. Nvidia's shares ended the session about 2% lower, bringing market value losses for the week to about $573 billion.Some analysts expect the next CEO to break from Huang's three-decade reign as the hands-on "chief conductor" who personally steered engineering roadmaps, geopolitical negotiations over exports to China and massive investments across the AI ecosystem.A potential shift toward a more institutional leadership structure would come as Nvidia faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and a growing consensus among US lawmakers to further restrict the company's chip exports to China.INSIDERS AND TECH TITANS IN THE RUNNINGAnalysts view Kress as a steady financial authority, while veteran engineer Ian Buck is seen as a top candidate after leading development of CUDA, the software platform that powers Nvidia's AI chips.Apart from Haas, external names discussed by analysts include AMD chief Lisa Su, who has navigated the key China market, and Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, whose memory chips power Nvidia servers.Other candidates cited by industry watchers include Marvell head Matt Murphy and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who oversaw the iPhone maker's in-house silicon development.Former Apple chief Tim Cook was floated by US President Donald Trump, as Nvidia's board evaluates whether to prioritize financial continuity, deep technical expertise, or experience running a global tech heavyweight.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Trump admits that suspension of flights in US may be linked to outdated equipment
news.text:
NEW YORK, November 14. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump admitted that the suspension of flights from all airports across the country may be linked to outdated equipment.

"This seems to be a situation where there's a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA [the US Federal Aviation Administration] relies on to keep planes in the sky," Fox News reporter Peter Doocy quoted the US leader as saying.

The journalist added that, according to Trump, the problem was not caused by a cyberattack or AI. "He says it does not seem like this is a cyberattack or AI or anything like that. I asked him a couple different ways, and he said it doesn't seem like that," Doocy said. "He said there's nobody taking credit [for what happened], which would be common if somebody did execute a huge cyberattack like this on critical infrastructure," the reporter noted.
news.summary: The problem was not caused by a cyberattack or AI, the US leader said
news.author: Tass

news.title: Rubio acknowledges in wake of GOP midterm losses that 'people are struggling' economically
news.text:
APSecretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged the economic struggles faced by Americans during his speech to conservatives

Washington: Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a sweeping speech to fellow conservatives on Friday evening acknowledging that Americans are struggling in the current economy, while also railing against what he called the "weaponization" of international law to constrain the U.S. from acting in its own interests.His comments to the conservative Federalist Society touched on a core issue of the midterm elections - economic pain - that U.S. voters pointed to as they delivered massive losses to Rubio's Republican Party."I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There's no doubt about it," he said. "The health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need."President Donald Trump often points to the stock market as evidence that the economy is doing well. But voters angry over higher costs gave Democrats control of Congress after blaming Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.Rubio's remarks had the overtones of campaign speech, though the former Florida senator has consistently refused to discuss whether he would seek the presidency in 2028 in a race that could pit him against Vice President JD Vance. Rubio gave another wide-ranging speech last month in Greece that focused on Western values and also appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America's top diplomat.Live EventsRubio on Friday defended the Iran war, arguing that it was necessary to stop the threat of the Islamic Republic obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he acknowledged that the unpopular conflict has driven up gasoline prices for Americans and other connected costs."It's not easy to address these things because it's not popular to address them," Rubio said. "It's difficult. And oftentimes it inflicts, you know, pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that."He also pointed to the need for American leaders to continue a tradition of ensuring the next generation is better off than those before them. Economic prosperity is "not self-perpetuating," he said, but an enormous undertaking that requires years and decades and is not accomplished "election cycle to election cycle.""That's the challenge before us now, because I do think there's a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off, and that can't happen. That's un-American," he said.Rubio also hit back hard on critics of Trump administration policies such as deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America, the January capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and strict immigration policies.He accused other countries and international organizations of trying to stymie the U.S. from acting in its own best interests by accusing the Trump administration of violations of international law."We've heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign policy decision or action of this administration," he said, describing it as "the weaponization of international law."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump plans Iran talks with Xi and Putin but not Ukraine, AFP reports
news.text:
President Donald Trump plans to discuss the Iran war, but not Ukraine, with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at a three-way meeting next week, a senior U.S. official said Friday.

The White House confirmed Friday that the leaders will meet Thursday, Nov. 19, alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. It will be the first-ever meeting of its kind among the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, the world's biggest nuclear powers.

The official briefed reporters anonymously and said Washington has a "whole other track" of talks with Kyiv and Moscow to end the Ukraine war, France 24 reported, citing Agence France-Presse. "China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official said.

U.S. envoys have spoken with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, according to the official. Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the leaders could use the Shenzhen meeting to discuss a potential Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.

Analysts interviewed by The Associated Press expect the meeting to produce few major breakthroughs and say symbolism will outweigh substance.

"I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Nuclear arms on the agenda

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," the official told reporters on a call. Trump has said the gathering would allow the leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of an agreement among the three countries on nuclear stockpiles.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous."

New START, the final nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, expired in February. That removed caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. Trump rejected Russia's call for another year on the agreement at the time, seeking a "new, improved and modernized" deal that would include China.

Pentagon estimates put China's nuclear arsenal at more than 600 warheads, while estimates for the U.S. and Russia exceed 5,000 each.

The senior official described the meeting as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" about nuclear disarmament and said no agreements are expected to be announced.

The official said it was time for China to "step up ... to the adult table" on nuclear stockpiles. The AP reported that Beijing has shown little interest in a nuclear pact, while administration officials acknowledged the subject is difficult for China.

Kremlin dismisses Yalta comparisons

The summit planning has prompted comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, at which U.S., British and Soviet leaders agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into occupation zones.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparisons earlier, saying agreements made in Shenzhen cannot be enforced on others. He said "the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order."

Trump's schedule

U.S. officials said Trump will depart Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for an Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit before traveling to Shenzhen.

Trump will have a working lunch and meeting with Xi on Thursday, their fourth meeting since he returned to power in 2025. No separate one-on-one meeting with Putin is on Trump's schedule.

Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk will accompany Trump to China but will not take part in the meeting with Xi and Putin.

news.title: Un nuevo escenario político: derrota, castigo electoral y reconfiguración ideológica
news.text:
Las recientes elecciones de medio término en Estados Unidos han redefinido el panorama político de esta nación. Contra muchas expectativas dentro del movimiento liderado por Donald Trump, los resultados reflejan un importante retroceso para el oficialismo. La magnitud del triunfo demócrata ha llevado a bautizarlo como un "tsunami azul", por la pérdida de escaños republicanos, sin dudas, desgaste político de una administración que había logrado una influencia considerable sobre amplios sectores del electorado.

Una parte importante de los votantes, incluidos independientes y antiguos simpatizantes republicanos, parece haber decidido expresar su descontento en las urnas. Entre los factores señalados como generadores de esta conducta se citan la política exterior, la guerra en Gaza, abusos contra la inmigración, el acceso a la salud, la protección ambiental y diversas acusaciones relacionadas con el uso y abuso del poder y la transparencia gubernamental.

Sin embargo, más allá de las razones inmediatas del voto, la pregunta que debe ocuparnos es qué rumbo tomará el país durante los próximos dos años, con un Congreso controlado mayoritariamente por la oposición. Este período tiene una importancia extraordinaria de cara a las elecciones presidenciales de 2028.

El filósofo y político italiano Antonio Gramsci afirmó hace un tiempo que: "La crisis consiste precisamente en el hecho de que lo viejo está muriendo y lo nuevo no puede nacer; en ese interregno aparecen una gran variedad de síntomas morbosos" (Gramsci, 1971, p. 276). Esta afirmación describe, de manera precisa, el momento la situación política actual de Estados Unidos.

Y es en este escenario que surgen dos preguntas categóricas.La primera es si Trump optará por vetar sistemáticamente las iniciativas del nuevo Congreso. Una estrategia de confrontación que podría fortalecer a sus seguidores más fieles, pero también proyectaría una imagen de bloqueo institucional si afecta decisiones económicas, presupuestarias o sociales de interés público.La segunda pregunta es si los demócratas deberían aprovechar su poder casi absoluto para impulsar una interpelación o un proceso de destitución (impeachment) al presidente. Esto ayudaría al fortalecimiento institucional, pero también podría fortalecer el discurso de victimización política que ha sido una de las principales banderas del trumpismo.

Al mismo tiempo, algunos sectores republicanos podrían concluir que la permanencia de Trump dificulta la reconstrucción del partido con miras al 2028. En ese contexto, figuras como J. D. Vance, u otros aspirantes presidenciales, podrían comenzar a posicionarse como alternativas para la próxima etapa del conservadurismo estadounidense.

Más allá del enfrentamiento entre republicanos y demócratas, existe una batalla dentro del Partido Demócrata. Estas elecciones, además de representar un revés para el trumpismo, revelan una disputa ideológica dentro de esta organización política. 

Durante años, los sectores moderados han dominado la dirección partidaria. Hoy, sin embargo, las corrientes progresistas y socialistas democráticas parecen ganar influencia con propuestas centradas en la justicia económica, los derechos laborales, la expansión de servicios públicos, la reforma migratoria y la lucha contra el cambio climático.

La cuestión es si este avance representa una reacción temporal contra el gobierno o el inicio de una transformación ideológica más profunda. Para algunos analistas, existe un cambio generacional favorable a una mayor intervención del Estado y a políticas orientadas a reducir las desigualdades. Para otros, se trata de un fenómeno coyuntural que podría revertirse una vez desaparezca el factor Trump.

Desde una perspectiva filosófica, esta tensión recuerda la idea de Hegel (1977) de que el cambio histórico emerge de las contradicciones que atraviesan una sociedad. La confrontación entre visiones opuestas no necesariamente anuncia una ruptura, sino la búsqueda de un nuevo equilibrio político.

El escenario actual está proyectado hacia 2028.Estados Unidos podría entrar en una etapa de polarización grave, marcada por bloqueos legislativos, reacomodos partidarios y una intensa lucha por el liderazgo político.Los republicanos deberán decidir si su futuro continúa ligado al liderazgo de Trump o si apuestan por una nueva generación. Los demócratas, por su parte, tendrán que resolver la creciente tensión entre moderados y progresistas, cada vez más acentuada.

Este panorama encaja en las palabras de Maquiavelo, cuando expresó: "No hay nada más difícil de emprender, más peligroso de conducir ni más incierto en su éxito que iniciar un nuevo orden de cosas" (Machiavelli, 2005, cap. VI, p. 21).

Las elecciones han cambiado las piezas del tablero, pero la verdadera lucha no será únicamente por el control del Congreso o de la Casa Blanca, sino por la definición del proyecto político e ideológico, encabezado por una generación contestataria, que dominará a Estados Unidos durante la próxima década.
